Question: What existing invention do you believe you could improve and how?
Answer: Other people write diaries. I have books full of ideas, gathered over the past 40 years, full of ideas how to make things better. Where to begin. If I am aware of its existence, I have had thoughts on how to improve it. It is my superpower. In theory, I could say, show me any object, and I can do a better one, and you’ll have my response within the day; as a 3D model if you wish. I am an industrial designer, and now work for the Swedish government as an innovation advisor. Some of my ideas have over the years become reality, because other people also thought of them, and I am rarely surprised by things that pop up on the market, because usually, I will have thought of that solution before. I used to think it could make me rich and famous, but the fact is that the world actually hates new ideas and will only ever resort to them when there is no other way, or when massive marketing efforts have been undertaken to make it palatable. Industry does not want my stuff, either, because they usually have their own plans. It would be my dream to meet someone who says “Chris, what inventions have you got? Let’s have an agreement, I send you a challenge, and you send me stuff, and I’ll get it patented and marketed, and we’ll see where it takes us.” I actually believe people like that, who could be my perfect partner in the business of marketing my inventions, exist. Somewhere out there, there will be a friendly, Chinese multimillionaire who is supremely well-connected and a little bored and likes the idea of carrying these little surprise packages to his fellow millionaires, who may try and implement the odd one in one of their factories. I’d be totally game for that! And I have stuff like that like lying around everywhere. Anybody want a…: Here, for fun, some of my ideas as computer models: Rocking chair with variable angling extent: Modular buffet table with integrated heating element: Telescopic couch table: Air Futon: Water minimising bathtub: Water boiler with variable temperature settings: Storm safe umbrella: Silicone glasses: Stair climbing suitcase with integrated chromebook: Am I crazy to just share these here? No! I’ve got hundreds and hundreds more of these, and I have these ideas over a glass of chardonnay on my couch, and I do these models over another glass of chardonnay on my couch, and nobody ever does anything with my ideas anyway, so, there. And I can always have new ones. If only I had TRACTION. Someone who sees the opportunity here and takes that stuff off me and does something with it. And perhaps my best invention is my Idea Generator. Feel free to try it! All you need to do is to choose one word per heading, and that gives you your challenge. Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is Swedish Lapland expensive?
Answer: Once you’re there, it’s not so bad. Relatively normal, Swedish prices. A friend of mine lives there, and she is actually of the opinion that it can be cheaper to live there than in the south of Sweden - but she is one of those outdoorsy people who likes to live in a cottage without electricity, and makes her coffee over an open fire. Let’s take a look at some prices. If you live there, you would of course be heating most of the year, so that is a factor to consider. On the other hand, the already relatively low power prices of Sweden (they are about half of what they are in Germany or France), are even lower in the north, so that may not be such a big thing. I live in a similar climate a bit further south and pay on average 2500 SEK a month for elctricity, but we heat and cook and make hot water with it, and have no oil or gas. My friend in the north tells me it’s similar for her, whenever she lives in a house with electricity, which she does during the colder part of the year (she’s a professional house sitter). And then, there’s the transport thing. Sweden is sparsely populated as it is, but the North is positively empty. If you ever want to go some place, like shopping, or having something repaired, you will be driving. And I mean, far. A liter of gasoline currently sits at about 21 SEK, and a liter of diesel at 23. If you drive to the nearest shopping mall with your good old Volvo 740, maybe 50 kilometers away, that adds SEK 200 to your pastrami. An electric car could make sense here, provided it has enough range in winter.

Question: How do you deal with someone with a big ego?
Answer: In my experience, someone with a big ego is really just scared to be ignored or misunderstood or forgotten. I would just placate the hell out of them. You’ll see, they won’t even notice. Instead, they’ll think of you as a really nice person who needs to be a part of their life. In essence, imagine you’re the whisperer of some megalomaniac narcissist despot monster. Play it right, and you can have gold, convertibles, and oysters till the cows come home, or till the big guy gets whacked. It has worked really well for me all my life, because I have, for some reason, been surrounded by people like that nonstop. The main thing is to make sure you seem so harmless and hapless and naive that the instigators of the palace revolt don’t come for you afterwards. The tyrant’s stupid pet, basically. With big eyes and cute whiskers. There, now you know the secret of my success. I’m a sycophant. I think it’s a high art. Especially when you’re being a sycophant with long term survival plans that go beyond the life span of the guy with the big ego.

Question: What is European to you, and why?
Answer: “European”, to me, is a value set. It combines a love of the finer things in life (literature, science, classical music, wine, cuisine) with societal responsibility (universal healthcare, pension system, unemployment insurance, unions, good work life balance), and a lot of freedom for the individual to pursue whatever religion, sexuality, or lifestyle they choose. There is a certain set of aesthetics that comes with that, which I would describe as sophisticated and well-developed, with often profound scientific or cultural references. I have yet to find a place outside Europe where this occurs with such intensity, perhaps with the exception of New Zealand, Canada, and Australia. I also find Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay quite good for these, as well as Japan. Some of these are actually trying to be European, it seems to me. Especially Argentina. Of course “European” could be defined in other ways, too - geographically, historically, politically… but as a designer, these are outside my sphere of influence. To me, the following show unmistakably European sights: Yes, that’s me in a turtleneck and tweed jacket, wearing brogues, with the old BMW 3.0, in my village in Alsace at the time. There’s also a generous serving of Tarte Flambée and a pichet of Gewurztraminer in my belly. Very European.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Sweden has been ranked #1 in terms of individualism. What makes Swedish society so individualistic?
Answer: When you watch Swedish movies, or read Swedish books, you’ll find that the characters depicted there tend to be totally over the top. Extreme figures with exaggerated strengths and weaknesses, eccentric leanings, and exceptional views. Not for Swedish film makers or authors, the notion that the audience should be able to “connect” to them, that they should be like them, relatable, normal. The concept of a “normal” person is strangely absent in Swedish thinking, and it finds its continuation in the Swedish everyday attitudes some view as sheepish political correctness. It’s not. In my opinion, Swedes simply do not believe that people have much in common with each other. Like the stars in the universe. And that’s fun, and natural. And I think it’s because this country hasn’t been at war in over two hundred years. Not for them, the idea that people can be put in uniform and then become all the same, are to be treated all the same, and have the same values. This is a soft society that does not apply pressures. I think the Swedes have drifted far away from the uniformity most of us others have embraced over the centuries, and they just view others naturally now. Like a child would do.

Question: What do you see, feel, and experience for yourself when all foods and drinks are perfect?
Answer: Lovely question. I’ll say, when all foods and drinks are perfect, I feel balanced. Because nothing is too much, or too little. Appreciating this state in itself is an art form, because we are so used to pushing ourselves until we run into some barrier - until we’ve had more than enough, until we’ve had too much. So when you are providing such a finely balanced experience, you are always running the risk that your guests may not be equipped for it. So add another component to your hospitality: Education. When your guests know what you are going for, they are more likely to notice it when it happens.

Question: What do you wish you had done with your life?
Answer: Looking back with the knowledge I now have, I wish I had done one thing, and one thing only, a lot more: Proceeding with more consideration. My life has been such a frantic scramble of trying this and trying that, moving here and moving there, fighting for this cause and that cause, worrying here, worrying there. It wasn’t worth it. I should have stayed my course and made my choices more carefully, using stronger data, better advisors. There were plenty of good things in my life I dropped unnecessarily - and plenty of stupid ones I gave a go. It’s the one thing I can recommend to anyone: Do your homework properly. The things that are worth going for will still be there, even if you take crazy long.

Question: Which car is the most "designed for old people" of all time?
Answer: Designing a car with geriatric consideration is a high art. Most cars these days have a certain element of that - at least more so than they used to do, given that the customer base is getting older. It mostly shows in lighter doors that open wider, but also in higher seats and more headroom, as well as lighter steering and pedal activation forces. I nominate the Peugeot 1007 as the ultimate effort so far in building a car for older people. Its large, electric sliding doors are an amazing feature that completely alleviates the issue of losing one’s grip on a car door and slamming it into another, parked car (my old Pontiac still has a grannie memorial dent from my own grandmother to that extent), or having to wriggle out of a car in a tight spot while trying to prevent the door from touching. It’s also a very compact car with surprisingly spacious interior, high seating position, and lots of head room to ensure you get the entire hairdo inside every time. I’ve actually come very close to buying one when I lived in England, because I think it’s very cool.

Question: What is something that tourists do in your country that instantly identifies them as tourists?
Answer: Probably the number one give away of being a tourist in Sweden is to have a motor home. Granted, there are Swedes who have one, too. But that just makes them tourists in their own country, doesn’t it. Not many drive these vehicles because they are so nippy around town, or because they need a stove with them, on the way to work. The next corpus delicti is this: German Brezen. Usually available only in supermarkets like Lidl or Aldi, and Germans fall upon them like cats upon tuna. For all their love of Sweden, living without these things seems to be very, very hard for them, and when you have a rejoicing family with a pile of these and little else in front of you at the cashier, you know they wouldn’t be locals - to whom these are mysterious items, entirely without cinnamon. And finally, elk warning signs. I won’t show an image, because it is their absence that reliably betrays the prior visit of a tourist. You drive to work, as you do, and one day, the sign is gone. Probably adorning some home office wall in Bad Homburg or Göppingen by the time you notice. The problem has taken on such proportions that the government has given the green light to selling these signs in shops now, to little avail. After all, it’s like buying fish in the supermarket instead of pulling out the prey oneself.

To me, they were simply lightly built cars from the VW shelf of componentry, with plasticky interiors, and mostly known for terrorizing the fast lane with an ever aggressive presence. As the 1990s went by, there they were, still on the roads. No rust, going strong. And then came the Naughties, and the 2010s… meanwhile, in Sweden in 2022, we see these cars still doing heavy winter duty in arctic weather, looking and running like new. To be fair, they are good to drive, as I’ve found out for myself in the 1990s, when a friend of mine in Canada had a 100 2.3 E. Very satisfying engine sound from that 5 cylinder motor, and generally good ergonomically. I still don’t like them, but I tip my hat.

Question: Do you need a car to get around in Sweden?
Answer: Let’s put it this way: You can get around Sweden without a car, no problem. You can live here fine without owning a car, too. The trains and buses are good, as are the airplanes, bicycles, kayaks, ferries, and shoes. Something will usually be there to take you further. But a car gives you a level of mobility and spontaneity the others wouldn’t. With that, you can come and go as you please, and far, too. If you absolutely want to, you can cross Sweden from south to north in two days, using a car, deciding where and when you stop for how long along the way. That tells you something about the power of having a car with you. You could even sleep in it. But if you plan your trip well, there’s no reason why it shouldn’t work out just as well using trains and a bicycle.

All Sweden. So that part is simply down to nature. Sweden occupies similar natural environments as the states mentioned above, and it is similarly empty. So what do you do with a mostly empty country in the north, with lots of wood in it, and a few houses? You build some straight roads, and some simple houses made from boards, and paint them, so they stay there. Looks like this: And what kinds of cars do you drive on those straight, wide roads that get bumpy from the frost every winter? Well, big, wide, soft ones, of course. Volvos and Saabs will work, but Cadillacs and Lincolns work even better: And then, in that big, empty country, what else is there to do? Probably just getting cozy at home, thinking of ways to improve things further, come up with a few great new solutions for problems one could even build in a shed and turn into a startup… maybe distill some spirits… go fishing, eat high calorie foods… There, recipe to make both the US and Sweden. Makes some good Canada, too. Now add some mutual inspiration in the form of immigration and movies, and we have two pretty similar places.

Question: What is Chris Ebbert's specialty?
Answer: I am an industrial designer by way of a bachelor’s degree in industrial design, and a transportation designer via my master’s degree. I have also been known to specialize in innovation, which not all of my colleagues in the described fields do. But mainly, I teach these things at university these days. These professions seem to cause never ending confusion, and people have been thinking of me as all sorts of things, starting with a “graphic designer” to an “engineer”, and all kinds of others in between. So I’ll explain what they really are, and what I really am, within those backgrounds: Industrial Design: A profession from the design field (not engineering! I know, the English language tends to lump them together, but shouldn’t). Specialized in creating new concepts intended for mass production, with a particular focus on the needs of the user, ergonomics, life cycle management, trend analysis, aesthetics, and brand identity. This sets my work apart from the work of engineers, because even though I take into account the requirements of manufacturing and engineering, they are not my main focus. An industrial designer creates the more “soulful” aspects of the product, that which makes the customer fall in love with it - the way it looks, feels, handles, behaves. It’s a profession with plenty of artistic input. We draw, sketch, model, animate, build mock-ups. Typical industrial designers are for example Dieter Rams or Giorgio Giugiaro. Transportation Design: A profession that is even more artistic. We specialize in making vehicles look great. You could say our job is to make sculptures on wheels. We are the people who work in the car industry to create the beautiful exteriors and interiors of new vehicles. Again, we sketch and draw a lot, we build 3D CAD models in software like Alias or Rhino, and we create full scale plasticine models of interiors and exteriors of cars from a material we call “clay” (but which is really industrial plasticine). These shapes are then used to create body panels or interior panels. It can take a few of us months to get these shapes right. It is not at all easy, because it is really an exercise in compromise. Generative Design software is expected to make a big difference for us soon. Typical transportation designers are for example Sergio Pininfarina and Giovanni Bertone. Innovation: I got my first patent when I was 13, and later also became an innovation advisor in the service of the government of Sweden. One might expect that a designer will be into innovation, but strangely, one can actually get away without being invested in it much. Still, it’s considered better when a new design really is innovative - which is just another way of saying that the new thing represents an improvement over the old thing. I consider it my specialty also with my students to be the guy who always expects innovation to be part of a new design - which means I usually give those of my students a hard time who come to me with purely cosmetic solutions. To me, that just never does it. I have started my PhD in Innovation Management, but have yet to come to an end with it. Maybe when I’m retired. And all wrapped up into one, you could say I am simply teaching industrial design at university, with my personal spin of mandatory innovation as an added flavour.

Question: Why is kebab so popular in Europe?
Answer: There must be a version of the concept “meat wrapped in bread” in just about any culture. Hamburgers in the US, sandwiches and pies in Britain and its Commonwealth, Wurschtsemmel in Germany and Austria, smörgåsar in Sweden and the rest of the Nordics, chivitos on the Rio de la Plata delta, etc. But kebabs do one thing the others don’t take to the same length: Complexity. The kebabs you can buy in your average kebab shop in Germany or Sweden can be loaded up in ways perhaps only the American chain Subway has ever tried to rival. If I want my kebab with fifty different things, I can have my kebab with fifty different things. Sauces, salads, pickles, you name it, it’s astonishing. In Germany, they will ask you (enter Turkish accent) “mit alles?”, which is grammatically wrong, but the correct way to order a kebab, and I do respond with “mit alles”. That gives me a bread type that is superior in appeal to the spongy things the westerners come to the table with, a grilled rotisserie meat of a higher perceived quality than the minced space cows that make up American or German processed wonders, lovely sauces with a touch of the Mediterranean that presumably contain far less rocket fuel than the production optimized things you get in little plastic boxes in your bag, and finely chopped, raw veggies that bulk up the whole thing to the point where you could be forgiven for thinking you’re eating something healthy. Have you tried eating till you are full on western fast food? I know people who’ve been trying for decades and are still not done, but have taken on frightening dimensions in the process. A kebab will actually make you feel full eventually. In short, kebabs outclass their contenders in quality, healthiness, and ability to actually fill you up. (My local kebab bar from the inside).

Question: Do we know anything about the future?
Answer: There is only one thing we can say with certainty about the future: None of it will be exactly like it once was. Everything is in such a state of flux in this universe that we can pretty much assume that everything we know will eventually be different. Unfortunately, that’s where the certainties stop, and we need to resort to other methods to try to make predictions about how things could become: None of these are “knowing” though. The longer I look into methods to predict the future, and how useless they are, the more I tend to believe that not knowing the future must be one of the most important aspects of human existence. It’s like a game. If you don’t know what’s going to happen, what kinds of decisions will you make? It teaches you a lot about yourself, your values, and your character.

Question: Is this true? In Sweden, people at work don't want to have anything to do with their co-workers when work is done? Swedes would never even consider having a drink or dinner with co workers?
Answer: By comparison to Asian ways, you may find the Swedes a bit like that, maybe. When I worked in China, it was very common to socialize with colleagues, even on weekends. That, unless it’s a strictly private thing without any work ties, would be unheard of in Sweden. Here, work is work, and stays there. A very clear partition is drawn there. I do have dinners with colleagues every now and then, because we happen to also be good friends. But that’s not the case for everybody in the work force, and what’s more, there is no expectation that you do that just to be a good colleague. At the base of this is probably a generally accepted standard of professionalism. To be able to act professionally toward one another in everyday contexts, it is necessary to keep that perspective. It’s a different story when one changes jobs; at that stage, an ex colleague can absolutely become a closer friend one shares more of life’s aspects with, without endangering any professional relationship. It’s nothing unusual, just a normal, western stance as you’d find it in France, the US, UK, or Germany, too.

As long as we can live with the consistently observable pattern of actions and manifestations of something, or someone, we are ok with them even when we don’t get the background. That sort of mindset is pragmatic, so perhaps pragmatism also helps. You may say “but where are we as individuals in all that?” Simple: Hopefully, we are experiencing the same treatment by the other. Question: Are Europeans, especially Germans, panicking over the coming winter considering Russia is about to cut off their gas supply?
Answer: Germans never panic. Instead, we live in denial until the situation gets so bad, it has to be embraced as something we either deserve or can see as a test of our soul, or a proof of the existence of extraterrestrial life or some conspiracy theory, or just a thing no one can do anything about, ever, except the government, and they better hop to it. I don’t live in Germany anymore, because I’m not like that, so they eventually threw me out. Or I threw myself out, or something. A jolly party is bad company when you’re a suspicious grouch. I’m a prepper at heart. I’m one of those people who immediately get suspicious when things go perfectly, because hey, there’s GOT to be a hitch to that, someone give me some boxes, I’ll start stockpiling sauerkraut while the going’s still good. Talking to my friends and relatives in Germany, and looking at their social media posts, you’d be forgiven for thinking Germany has just discovered the recipe for free energy. There’s jolliness and merrymaking going on, big meals are cooked, exotic holiday plans are extolled on, and rooms are painted in exquisite colours. Presumably all as an advance compensation for a winter which will be cold, expensive, and meager on many levels, I try to rationalize it to myself. But I know I’m wrong. Having spent a whole childhood in Germany, I know Germans feel safest with their heads firmly lodged in the sand as disaster approaches. It’s the only explanation for why there could be so much disaster there in the first place, and why there is now again - it takes a really nice sand pit to enter such profound energy dependencies with historically unsound partners as they have done. Look how nice the hair stays when the head isn’t in the sand. Don’t put it there, folks. Get prepping. And I don’t mean Boeuf Bourguignon. There’s actually a famous, historical figure to illustrate this attitude: Der deutsche Michel. “German Michael”, der deutsche Michel, is this bumbling, simple minded, happy go lucky guy who lives from day to day and stays firmly within his own bubble. He’s alive and well.

Question: How do people in Sweden (and overall cold climate countries) ventilate their houses? Do they open the windows?
Answer: Opening a window would be the standard approach for ventilation, yes. And the northern European classic of window mechanisms is this, the inward-leaning window opening for ventilation (the Germans call it “Kippfenster”): You can see it in use in this image, where the very left window is opened in this way. I have not seen this used much elsewhere. You see it pretty much everywhere in Germany, Austria, Sweden, France, and so on, but I have never come across it in Canada, the US, China, India, the UK, or New Zealand. It has a good number of advantages, such as: People even leave these open as shown while going to work. There are burglar proof versions of these, and they actually are quite burglar proof just by default. Other than that, houses are built to “breathe” to a certain extent, of course. There is a natural attrition of air at all times, through door seals and window seals. Cat doors are actually an enormous ventilation gate, I find, to the point where I’ve found myself compelled to build an air lock for our cat door. You probably won’t find this anywhere else. Many houses actually have ventilation ducts for passive ventilation built in, not unlike cars. Look closely at the gables of some houses, and they may have a little grid there. The thing is of course that ventilation must continue even when it is so cold outside that you can’t open any windows.

Question: What's an invention that you are personally affiliated with or responsible for?
Answer: My first patent was an apparatus that can draw straight lines on any surface. I was 13 when I got it, and 12 when I applied. It made me Europe’s youngest patent owner at the time. It would do straight lines on things such as model train set landscapes, car bodies, boat hulls, you name it. But also fluffy, wet, rough, or textured surfaces. Some of the journalists who wrote about me described the device as a three legged compass, which fits quite well. It’s a part of the registry of German patents to this day, with the code DE DE3507053C2 19.02.1987 · Issued Feb 28, 1985. It never made me rich, at least not directly. What it did do was to convince my school that I deserved a bit of a break regarding my colossal failures in the natural sciences, and was probably safe to be let loose on society despite them. And it taught me at a very early age how innovation validation works. My invention warranted a patent because nobody in recorded history had ever built a thing like I had, and it had a reasonable purpose, and could be manufactured according to specifications. This theme put me on my professional track for life. I went on to become an industrial designer and innovation advisor, and now teach industrial design at university level. It is a bit odd that a 13 year old needs to get a patent to be allowed to proceed through high school, but then, these were times when ADD and “dyscalculatoric school difficulties” didn’t exist. I was just a hopeless maths student with inexplicably high arts and language marks until I got a patent. I may owe my career to my patent.

Question: What are some of your amazing inventions?
Answer: Well, how about a house that uses the summer’s energy in winter? Endlessly. This works forever, or at least for as long as your solar panels or wind generator continue to make electricity: Build two water reservoirs with water that is laced with antifreeze on top of each other, and fill one. This is a closed system. Using solar, pump the water into the high tank over the summer. During winter, generate electricity from that water using a turbine and collect the water again in the bottom tank. Imagine digging a very deep excavation. 80 x 80 x 160 meters. Into it, you put one large water reservoir, 80 x 80 x 80. Then another one just like it on top. Then you build a house - on top, or next to it. Fill one reservoir with water and antifreeze. Ideally the top one, saves you a summer’s worth of pumping. Then you install a water turbine that can generate electricity from the water in the top tank, and an electric pump that is powered by solar, and designed to pump water from the bottom tank to the top tank. Any time a power consumer is turned on in the house, the turbine starts going, releasing water into the lower tank, and making electricity. And any time there’s sunlight, the pump brings some of that water back into the top tank, so it may actually never be empty, as there’s always sunshine, also in winter and spring and autumn. The size is enough to generate one year’s worth of electricity just from the contents of the reservoir.

It suddenly became obvious to me that that thing could be used for scheduling everything in life, and I started doing so. I’m a different person now. All I need to do is pop it into that calendar while I still remember it. And remember to keep checking that calendar during the day.

Question: In the Scandinavian countries, would people be more impressed if you spoke French or German?
Answer: Both English and French are fairly commonly learned at high school level in Sweden, so if one speaks one of these, or even both, you are just assumed to have been a good kid who made the most of their education. Those choosing French may more easily be considered interested in France, and all the gourmet pleasures that come with it. If I had to hire a young person as a trainee chef, I might actually prefer one who speaks French, because I can feel they may have an affinity to what really matters in the field. And those choosing German may have a more business attuned tendency, since Germany is one of Sweden’s more important business partners, and the language also opens up Austria, Switzerland, and Luxembourg.

Question: Why does Sweden not have shootings despite having lots of guns?
Answer: Many countries are armed to the teeth, yet we don’t hear about shootings from there as we do from some. There are shootings in Sweden, but they tend to be of the mafia type - rivals taking each other out. The “lone gunman against the society” thing is not an issue here. In Sweden, we have a pretty serious level of armament in the general population. It’s perfectly common and legal to own fire arms here. But they are generally accepted to be for sports and hunting, not for self defense, or to bring down the government if you feel so inclined. The whole premise is different, because the attitude and motivation differs.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Why are people saying it is so difficult to make friends (as adults) in Sweden as if it’s a unique thing?
Answer: I agree with your sentiment there. It is odd, isn’t it? Honestly, whenever I spot one of those questions that seem to showcase how some nation or culture is doing something unpleasant, or generally is unpleasant in some way, I tend to suspect it’s a trolling effort. These days, the internet is used so much to cook up myths and bend reputations to fit an emerging, political agenda somewhere that could benefit from its population holding less sympathy toward the affected society. So that’s why I think people are “saying that” these days - 50% of these statements are trolling efforts, and probably almost the entire other half of it are echoes of those. For the tiny percentage that may still be left as authentic, my answer would be this: Sweden is a European country. In Europe, “friends” are something children make, and they may last for an entire lifetime. You won’t find some 50-year old like me pining for new friends. I’ve got my fill. Sure I have made new acquaintances, and some cultures may call those “friends”. They are people who sometimes eat with us, or we eat with them; some do things for us, and we for them. But growing up, my childhood friends were of a more intense kind. These were resilient relationships that came with crisis and went through phases. They could bounce back. Adult friendships are more fragile, and are of a “one mistake, and you are out” type. It’s simply the story of adult life, and of cultural differences in definition of what a friend is.

Question: Why is it considered poor manners to ask where someone is from?

Maybe we could argue benevolently by saying it sounds wise and gracious to want to take into account the cultural dimension, but the sad fact is that stereotypes just don’t work as background information, and very few of us actually have the kind of insights and experience to really stand up to scrutiny when it comes to forming an opinion ...

Question: Why do people make fun of English cuisine?
Answer: I attribute the undeserved, low key reputation of English cuisine to Britain’s own modesty. When you come to England, you will struggle to find any “English restaurants”. They do exist, but not everywhere, contrary to, say, Germany or France, who quite proudly serve up their own foods as a main fare at many ventures. Personally, I think it’s unfortunate, because English food really is quite nice. In fact, I think of it as a historically interesting cuisine that quite authentically showcases what food in Europe would have been like for centuries, before the influx of Mediterranean, Asian, and Middle Eastern cuisines in the 20th century. Another factor that may well have harmed its reputation is that only select aspects of it survive in public view as fast food offerings, which of course never tend to occupy major chapters in a country’s culinary claims to fame. You can’t build a solid record with Michelin based on chippies and pub fare. Especially with exotic contenders making a stronger case for themselves. English cuisine lacks visibility, and venues.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What does “tak tak” mean in Swedish?
Answer: “Tak tak” means “roof roof”, and has no actual use in real Swedish other than perhaps as a safe word. But it sounds the same as “tack tack”, which means “thanks thanks”. Doubling words is the Swedish way to soften the message, also visible in “hej hej” (hello/ bye as in “toodaloo”).

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Are Swedes stoic?
Answer: No, I wouldn’t call the Swedes stoic. Not in the Japanese sense that is so famously showcased in one of my favourite movies, Tampopo, where a truck driver helps a restaurant owner achieve greatness in noodle soups. Stoicism, in a way, is a forceful thing, even a passive aggressive thing, in my opinion, because it requires to make an effort to subdue emotion and reaction. The Swedes though, I’d describe as simply calm, natural, resting within themselves. These are people who are comfortable with themselves and their environment, free from many of the fears and pressures that put most of us others on crooked rails for stretches of our lives. I sure count myself toward that. I was one obtuse weirdo before coming to Sweden, but since then, I’ve somehow managed to find my equilibrium. It’s like Sweden is an environment that causes all neuroticism to fizzle out and disappear.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: When and how did Sweden become so Americanized?
Answer: I hereby offer a cultural hypothesis: Sweden and the US have always been closely related, and simply represent parallel developments along similar lines. In other words, Sweden has always been an alternative reality to the US. This probably started becoming most evident in the first part of the 20th century, and proceeded to develop well into the second half of it, noticeable till today. There is a cultural relation, and a technical one. Culturally, Sweden has always been like much of the US because it is a similar environment, with lots of forests, a belief in equality, individuality, social mobility, and freedom. This goes back hundreds of years, and it may well be that the Swedish immigration waves of the late 1800s actually brought, or at least reinforced this influence in the US. And both countries have always believed that everyone deserves to live well- it’s just that one of them figured out the angles to make it happen across all levels of society a little better so far. Technically, both Sweden and the US have always been places that believed in early technology adoption, innovation, and bringing about betterment for society through new processes and pol...

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How do you dress for Swedish culture?
Answer: I would say “smart to casual” always does it. At work, with friends, when out and about. And don’t forget that the climate tends to call for astronaut style outfits during much of the year, so there is really only a small leeway when it comes to considerations of style. There is very little sense of “correct dress” here. You could walk the streets of any Swedish city dressed as a Fuzzy, as Lawrence of Arabia, as a cowboy, or in a three piece suit, there will be no reaction by the public. Whatever you wear, it will be assumed that you have good reason to wear it. Some images, showing people in real life:

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What is the point of Nordic walking?
Answer: Personally, I have come to the conclusion that Nordic Walking mostly serves to prove the point how pleasant its diametrical opposite, Southern Comfort, is. I mean, look at it. There you are, limping along with two sticks, as if you’re one season late and have lost your skis. By contrast, you could be sitting there, with an orange flavored beverage, on the rocks, watching the dolphins.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Why don't people in Europe buy air conditioners?
Answer: There is a deadly fear of power bills in Europe. I’m not kidding. My own example included. When I lived in Germany, my average monthly power bill was about 50 Euros, and it raised the same hackles as income tax raises with Americans. It seemed an existential threat to my existence. Not because it was that much money, but because it just seemed so… imposed. There is nothing you can do about your power bill, and there is nothing you can do about your income tax. Maybe the power bill is 50 Euros this month, but it could be 500, or 5000, if the mysterious powers that be so decide. Of course it won’t be, but the feeling is there. I paid 500 dollars a month in New Zealand and 200 Euros in France and 3000 kronor in Sweden and never blinked, but somehow, most of Europe just hasn’t got the nerve to man up to a power bill. And that’s how it is - an air conditioner eats power, and costs money. And the impossibility to calculate and monitor that cost as it occurs is too much for most Europeans. They believe they will be bankrupt after one month of using an air conditioner. I suggest installing power meters that display Euros, and eventually, Europeans will understand and learn to trust air cons. To illustrate the psychology behind it, I know a German lady here in my village in Sweden who heats with fire wood because it saves her 80 Euros a month over electricity. Well, that’s just crazy. She could very easily afford a much higher bill than that, but she is of the opinion that “the power bill MUST NOT BE OVER 100 EUROS, ever.” To the death. It’s a psychosis.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How long does it take to drive from Stockholm to the northernmost point in Sweden (Abisko)?
Answer: Two full days. Three if you stop along the way, and four to five if you really enjoy the trip. What this map does not show you are the pretty stops along the way you may want to take advantage of, namely Sundsvall, the High Coast, Umeå, and Lapland. It’s a four hour drive from Stockholm to Sundsvall, which I think is a really nice place to have lunch and spend the afternoon, perhaps going to the beach on Alnön: One night spent there, maybe eat hotpot at Canton, then on to Umeå, also about four hours. You could also put in another stop at Höga Kusten, the “High Coast”, which is spectacular. Personally, I could see myself spending a lifetime there: Next day, five hours to Jokkmokk: And the day after that, another four leisurely hours to Abisko. That’s the way to do that trip.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How are people coping with the heat in Europe?
Answer: Some of us are dealing with the heat by sheer luck. For some reason, we’ve been seeing low temperatures and rain for six weeks here now in Östersund, Mid Sweden, while my family in Germany and Austria is boiling at temperatures between 38 and 41 Celsius. I am immensely grateful for being up here. In fact, I am currently sitting in my basement TV room with my cats, running a heater. Studies actually predict that my part of Sweden is going to be more and more like that. Given the brutal heat further south, I am really glad to be here. As for my family, it seems that my parents are often retreating to the basement of their 1970s row house in Germany, or taking a dip in a lake in Austria. As temperatures sink lower in the evening, they sit outside in the breeze with a glass of white wine.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is it worth bringing a car to Sweden?
Answer: If you are coming in from a European or North American country, it may be worth bringing a car. I find that used cars in Sweden tend to be more expensive than in Germany or Italy, and they also tend to have higher mileage at the same price. On the other hand, driving in Sweden means you’ll want a set of studded winter tires, and a fitted engine block heater, as well as an interior fan heater. Acquiring all of these for some four digit Mercedes from Italy may be more than it’s worth. But if the car is something rare and special, like a Toyota FJ Cruiser, or an Avalon Hybrid, or a Camaro, it can be worth it, because these cars simply don’t exist here.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is there a country that you wish you lived in that wasn't the US?
Answer: I love the US, and live there vicariously by watching one American movie after another. I enjoy the environment, the language, the cars, the spirit. Better Call Saul, Breaking Bad, The Big Lebowski, Fargo, Pulp Fiction… I often wish I was back there. Maybe teaching at Berkeley or in Boulder, driving an old Lincoln, living in some weatherboard house from the 50s, eating burritos and enjoying the thrill of four way stops. But I have left 25 years ago, and it is likely going to stay that way. When I lived there, I was quite nervous. There are many pressures there that don’t exist in Europe, where I’m originally from. So the only reason for me to live in the US would be romantic. And it’s a very good reason, granted. Life is too short not to indulge in a bit of adventure. But I’ve done the US now, and if I didn’t live in a place now that really ticks my boxes, I might consider these: Seems like life is also too short to get enough of some places. These are enough to spend a lifetime in.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How do you deal with somebody who comes off too strong?
Answer: I’ve been around a few cultures where coming on strong is the way. It’s annoying, isn’t it? But there is one simple way to deal with it. We are all adults, and someone who comes on strong usually does so making a promise. Hold them to it. You can’t lose. Either they keep it, in which case, you are probably getting an anti gravity cruiser with Mach 15 capability by tomorrow evening; or you don’t, in which case a guy like that is vanquished for good.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Do you appreciate getting older more as you age or was younger better for you personally?
Answer: I’m only fifty, but I have observed a strange thing: The older I get, the better I get. Mentally, physically, personally. It’s probably not going to continue like that forever, because we do wear out and leave eventually. But so far, that has been my experience. I explain it with a very simple thing. The longer we are around, the more we figure things out. Granted, not all of us do. Many of us fall for all sorts of things and never disentangle ourselves from them, leading to doing worse mentally, physically, and personally way before age fifty. But I’ve always wanted to do well. I’ve always seen my body and my existence as something fragile, and deserving of proper maintenance. So I’ve always kept a close eye on the best possible methods to ensure it, and I think it is this mindset that makes it possible.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Are Swedes friendly at work?
Answer: Just a few days ago, I was sitting with a cup of coffee at a little outdoor café in the shadow of Stockholm’s city tower, chatting to two Austrian teachers who were in town with their students. They mentioned how remarkably helpful and nice they found the Stockholmers, and asked me if they were like that at work, too, given that I’d probably know, living here and all. To which I was able to say, without reservations, oh yes. If you work with Swedes, you are in a world of pleasantness. At least if you’ve worked elsewhere. I sure am very grateful. Which is not to say that you’ll never encounter any adversity, of course. But the Swedish way of dealing with it is smoother than in most places, and what’s probably more important: You’ll never see any tantrums or complete flip-outs like in Germany, France, the US, or China. Swedish culture is generally conflict avoidant and harmony seeking, so despite the many curses you may be hearing, rest assured, you are not likely going to have anyone fly at you in a rage, ever. Work, career, and success also don’t occupy the same place as they do in many other countries, because income disparity is low, and there isn’t the same sense that you have to fight your way to the top, prevail, get promoted. In Sweden, private life takes precedence over work, and work is only a way to finance it. You can feel that. Work is not the real life here.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is it worth moving to Sweden for money?
Answer: Not really. Sweden is worth moving to for balance in life, not money. You can earn more elsewhere. The whole thing about Sweden is that it’s not all about money. Yes, you’ll earn about the same as in the UK, or New Zealand, or Canada. And like in those countries, taxation bites off a good chunk of your earnings and invests them into the system, for yourself, and for others. So if you have a family, you may find that it’s worth it, as it means that every one of them is automatically fully health insured, and can attend school and university with no tuition fee charged. But if you have no family, there’s almost no point, other than liking Sweden, which is what made me choose it. You’ll take home about the same percentage of your earnings as you do in most parts of the world. I’ve earned pretty much the same in England, France, Germany New Zealand, and the US, and in all of these, about 30% of what I earned was kept and went toward social expenditure. Well, actually, there was more bitten off in Germany. And in the US, it was 30% only because I had no health insuran...

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What are some safety concerns for tourists in Berlin?
Answer: Berlin is a very safe city, even by northern European standards. I’ve repeatedly visited, even with student groups, and the only trouble there ever was tended to be of the self made variety - getting drunk and losing one’s mobile phone or wallet, or getting thrown out of a hotel for turning rambunctious at 3 am and holding shoe throwing competitions in the corridors. Yes, these were British students. Other than that, nothing at all to be worried about. Do watch your stuff, as it is a big city after all, so it may find takers if left unattended. But it’s nothing like the perils of some places. There, just look at these images. They scream “harmless”, don’t they? Never mind the graffiti. It’s part of the whole Berlin thing. And watch out for calories, they are out to get you.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What is the most German item on your bucket list?
Answer: I have one guilty pleasure I really struggle to overcome, so I believe I may be in for it eventually: Old Mercedes-Benz. I have owned a good number of them, and not all of them were a good experience. But there are some I do trust, and it may well happen that I will eventually get one of these three models: American spec 300 CD Turbodiesel: American spec 300 SD Turbodiesel: W124 300 E: I find these models endlessly delightful, and very trustworthy.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How fast can you drive in Sweden?
Answer: There is a wide range of speed limits in Sweden. I’ve seen (all in km/h): In general, it is advisable not to exceed these limits too far. You will see locals pulling some stunt flight figures, but that’s usually because they know when the sheriff is on his lunch break, or they know where the speed camera is. I find it keeps harmonious relations best to sit at about 10–15% above any posted speed limit according to your car’s speedometer. It’s what everybody does. If you find yourself straying into unlawful speeds, this could get you bigger tickets at slower speed limits. Doing 50 in a 30 zone can spell absolute death to your driving licence, but doing 130 in a 110 zone is merely expensive. Could you, technically, drive faster? Hell yeah. Swedish roads are very much like French or American roads - straight, wide, good. I’d have no issues doing 300 on one of these with the right car, in summer, if it were legal. The only problem is that for all their straight looks, they can be very bumpy in spring time, as parts of them are sagging due to thawing frost under their surface. Then, you may need a new Ferrari soon.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What are some tourist traps in Sweden?
Answer: All traps in Sweden in which tourists are caught are humane, and of very good quality. I’ll say there is no “tourist trap” in Sweden of the kind one so easily finds oneself stuck in in places like Venice, Tijuana, or Prague. Attractions in Sweden tend to be of a caliber that draws local repeat visitors, too, not just tour bus passengers from Kyoto who will forever remember half frozen dumplings, 110 V heating blankets, or twenty dollar Cokes in other places. As for actual examples of places worth seeing in Sweden that might well have been turned into tourist traps elsewhere, here my favourites: JAMTLI, Östersund: GAMLA LINKÖPING: BOHUSLÄN Coast:

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is it normal behaviour for Swedish supermarket check out staffs not to say thank you (like part of their routines at checkout?)?
Answer: When you go through a Swedish checkout, the cashier will simply scan your wares, then wait for you to swipe your card and move on. They won’t give you the full hospitality treatment like in North America that may include polite inquiries into your health, a company slogan, and a wave goodbye with flowery proclamations of looking forward to soon being reunited at this counter with more purchases. Instead, you may get a friendly nod. If you say “hej då” as a farewell, they will be happy, and you can see it on their faces, but it may not be reciprocated. Swedish interactions presume inner harmony of all concerned as a default setting, so there is no necessity for vocalized assertions of benevolence every step of the way.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How can I use the heat of summer to heat my home in the cold of winter other than growing plants and burning them?
Answer: I would do this: Build two water reservoirs with water that is laced with antifreeze on top of each other, and fill one. This is a closed system. Using solar, pump the water into the high tank over the summer. During winter, generate electricity from that water using a turbine and collect the water again in the bottom tank.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How do you deal with culture shock in Sweden?
Answer: Everyone will have their own flavour of culture shock when coming to Sweden, of course, depending on where they are from. And therefore, reactions to it will be dependent on your culture of origin. For me as a German, it was easy. Sweden simply seems like an airier, more dignified Germany, with seasons and scenery like from one of those corny “Heimat” themed children's books of the early 1900s. So I've dealt with that by toning down my inner “Sturm und Drang” impulses, and just chilling the hell out. Others have it harder. My wife, Chinese from a city of 25 million, needs regular detention in large, neon lit shopping malls to deal with the terror of being surrounded by deep forests and big blue lakes. I am, in fact, writing this from a parking lot at Birsta shopping mall complex Sundsvall as the lady of the house has gone for retail therapy in the labyrinth of REAs. Hours ago. Then, there are my Arab friends from the film team, equally spooked by the wilderness, huddling over peppermint tea on a rug in their flat as moose and bears frolick outside, in the snow. Or my Canadian colleague, who misses having a French side on his breakfast cereal packaging, but otherwise feels just like at home.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Should I buy one of those Swedish $5000 houses in the middle of nowhere? Would I be able to spend summers there and work in a home office? How is the internet connectivity there?
Answer: I did, and it has been the best purchase of my life. Well, it was three times that price, fifteen years ago, and I was insanely lucky both with location and the shape it’s in. I’ve only replaced the roof and the heating system, which pretty much doubled my investment. But make no mistake about it, a cheap house can be an absolutely catastrophic sink hole for your money in many ways. A friend of mine bought one at five times the price, and has been having problems I didn’t even know existed - such as infestations with weird bugs, shifting foundations, collapsing roof beams, and badgers making their way in via subterranean mode. Internet is excellent where I am, but like I said, my house is in a village with very good infrastructure. On the whole, I can still recommend it, as long as you are sure that you can maintain it when you’re away. These houses usually stand for a certain place in their community, and tend to come with people who are often self appointed guardians who will gladly keep an eye on it for you, if you know how to connect. One thing you must absolutely have is internet banking, and it becomes light years easier once you have a Swedish bank account - which is very hard to obtain, unless you have a Swedish social security number. And getting one of those is on a whole other level.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: When does it get really warm in Sweden?
Answer: Let’s put it this way: Really warm days in Sweden, with temperatures between 25 and 30 Celsius, can occur in the months of June, July, and August. But they would not be considered the norm. 20 - 25 degrees may be considered the summer norm in much of Sweden. But some summers just don’t take off. So far, I would consider the summer of 2022 to be one such candidate. At least in Mid Sweden, where I live. Today, I went for a stroll through the woods at about 17 Celsius, and then went to pick up my wife at the railway station in the evening at 9 degrees Celsius. Just before that, I got off a video conference with my parents in Germany, still sitting in their garden at 29 Celsius late at night. That just doesn’t occur in Sweden. It stays civilized to chilled. So it’ll be nice, and it can even be warm for a few weeks at a stretch - I just spent a week in Stockholm sweltering at 26 to 20 Celsius all week long; it can be done. Do we really want it? Personally, no. If I can’t wear a tweed jacket, it’s too warm. Stockholm heat: Here, my place tonight, 600 km north of that: We are on the same latitude as Alaska, after all. Not even Gulf Stream magic can compensate much for that.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is Sweden a good place to live with climate change?
Answer: I am writing this on a July evening in Jämtland, Mid Sweden, at nine degrees Celsius outside as my brother and parents are sweltering in Germany and Austria at day temperatures between 33 and 39 Celsius. During the day, we had seventeen Celsius. This disparity is quite common between the two regions, I find, also in winter. When Germany is at around freezing point, we may see around minus fifteen. I went for a walk in the woods behind my house, dressed like a civilized person, perfectly comfortable. At such temperatures, without any freak spikes, life with the peculiarities of global warming is manageable. Another thing that’s reassuring is that the tectonics of Scandinavia are doing an odd thing: They are actually lifting the landmass out of the water at a rate that is quicker than that of sea level rise. So we may never need to worry about rising sea levels up here. What does worry me is the fact we are looking at a country that is largely covered in forest, and has increasing tendencies to forest fires. If there’s ever a seriously dry summer, there’s a lot of fuel here. This was in 2018, behind my village’s gas station: 2018 was an exceptionally fire prone year. Other issues places can have pertaining to global warming are of course to do with agriculture and soil erosion. Given the number of trees and lakes we have here, that’s not that much of a thing here, and then, there is a study I read recently that points out that Sweden’s climate is about to get wetter due to global warming. So I think it will actually balance out quite well, all things considered.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How is Sweden affected by climate change?
Answer: In practical terms, we see warmer temperatures and less snow than used to be the standard in the 20th century. This has resulted in Sweden’s southern half getting fairly mild, snow-less winters for the past twenty years. The North has seen less snow and higher temperatures, too, but there has also been an increase in precipitation, which is said to continue. So we could say the effect of global warming in Sweden has been: These are all things that affect life in very real ways, and when you check statistics, it checks out. Still, Swedish summers are not as crazy hot as they are in central Europe. I am sitting here in my hammock at a very comfortable 22 Celsius as my brother is boiling in Germany at 39, and my boss in Spain at 45. Nice as that may be, the village elders are telling me 12–15 used to be more common. That’s clearly a challenge to the fauna and flora. On the upside, the Scandinavian Plate is actually rising out of the ocean at a faster rate than sea levels, so Sweden is going to be one of those very few places on Earth where sea level rises will be a non-issue.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Why do so many people seem to find German culture and society unappealing?
Answer: Being German, at least on paper, this has vexed me all my life. It’s as if one immediately plummets in social market value once the words are spoken, “he’s German”. I attribute it to the holocaust. That was such a total blow to any respect Germany could possibly deserve, forever, and it is such a dark chapter, that it really acts like a quasar for any sympathy. It stands for the worst possible thing a society could do, and I am actually not surprised at all that everyone has had enough of Germany, forever. I have, too. When I heard the story, even though I was born thirty years afterwa...

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Are the Nordic countries much different from continental Europe?
Answer: Yes, I consider the Nordics quite different from continental Europe. Perhaps a little less so in terms of mentality and culture, but definitely in terms of environment. When you are in the Nordics, you may feel that the people are very much like the Dutch, or the French. But the environment is very different from continental Europe. It’s vast, wild, and brilliantly colourful. Where I live now reminds me mostly of Alaska, Patagonia, or Canada in general. Wide open expanses of deep blue, glittering water, deep old forests, and you can drive for hours without encountering a soul. You may at times think you have time traveled, because there’s just nothing up here to tell you what year it is. You wouldn’t get that, on the continent. I just took these before lunch today. Try that in Germany or Belgium.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Which ones are the best effects of spending the summer in a village, and why is that?
Answer: When you are in the village in summer, at least where I am, you will relax a lot. That’s because… : Just a few snapshots I took before lunch today: And in the end, the effect may well be that you decide you want to live like that for the rest of your life. I sure do.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How do the Swedes deal with heat?
Answer: The obvious answer is of course to strip off and hop into a lake. It’s very easy here, as the law gives anyone access to them, and it’s ok to hop in naked, too. So, no great preparations required, one can just act on impulse. Also, these lakes are often drinking water quality, so no fear of micro organisms. One of the problems with unusually high summer temperatures in Sweden is that the houses here are built to keep the heat in, not out. That makes sense in a climate where you are mostly heating, throughout the year. Luckily, we don’t tend to get the absolute furnace grade temperatures they have further south in Germany or France, so the situation is not entirely unbearable. While I visited my wife in Stockholm last week, temperatures there were edging close to thirty Celsius, and due to frequent rain showers, this occurred at a fairly high level of humidity. Whenever we came home to her apartment, it felt like it was even warmer inside the building than outside. We felt reminded of our years in Shanghai, always drenched in sweat. Here, this type of house - some 1980s construction, very common in Sweden’s suburbs: Air conditioning isn’t a well-known feature in Swedish households, so I daresay we had more hope in Shanghai to get comfy. At home in Jämtland, six hundred kilometers north of Stockholm, the climate is different though, so the question doesn’t really arise. Temperatures tend to be about five degrees lower than in Stockholm at all times, so a typical summer’s day usually sits at about 18 to 23 degrees Celsius. Today, it’s even just 11, on the tenth of July 2022. While that can happen, it is unusual. It’s been a very chilly, rainy summer so far. I will be barbecuing with friends today on the veranda, and we will have the fireplace going in the living room as we sit there in heavy, Norwegian sweaters and turtlenecks, sipping white rum. Personally, I love that sort of weather. In previous summers, we tended to have a problem with the upper rooms in the house getting too warm for comfort at night. The house is from 1952, and used to have a typical clay shingle roof which would get charged up with heat during the day, and then slowly gave off that heat during the night, as Adobe constructions also famously do. It was hard to find any rest, due to the heat, and we didn’t want to open the windows, because of the traffic of wildlife and pets - cats going in and out, birds doing the same, and so on. Things changed when we replaced the roof with a tin roof. The tin roof cools off very quickly as the sun sits lower above the horizon, and it’s been great since then in summer. Tin roofs are quite common in Sweden. Other ways to deal with the heat are of course to just stay outside, lightly clad, drink chilled things, and make use of it. We only get about a month or two a year where this can be done, after all.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: As you get older, what are some things that you realise?
Answer: I’m now 50, which is, by today’s standards, not really much of an elevated age. My parents, who are in their eighties and as fit as I am, still call me “young”. But looking back now, my impression is that there were certain paradigm shifts along the way. For me, they were as follows: * from about six to sixteen, I was a proper nerd. Name any car model, dinosaur, or country in South America, I knew all the data. And I believed that that was what mattered in life. * from about sixteen to twenty-six, I switched to a reckless storming mode. I believed I had certain talents, and needed to fight my way through, against the system, to be allowed to be in a place where I could thrive. I saw everything and everyone as being in my way, and that life was all about prevailing against the system. * from twenty-six to about thirty, I decided now it was time to make do on what I had achieved - and found it entirely insufficient. I had a big crisis, and changed career. I also changed my body, turning into an exercise buff, lost 43 kg, and went through a phase I would now call dangerously self hating. I understand today this was only possible because I had allowed people to manipulate me. But I believed, during those years, that a total sell-out of myself was the right way to live. * my thirties saw me in a slump. I basically decided I had nothing I wanted to live for anymore, but since there were people who appreciated me, I decided to just do whatever they wanted. I was useful, earned good money, went along. I was basically a living dead. And since that came with nice cars, nice clothes, nice homes, and general acknowledgement, I thought all was as it should be. * at the end of my thirties, that model collapsed. Not surprisingly, perhaps. Who wants to live with a yes-saying corpse, after all. And at about age 40, I came back to life. Suddenly, I knew where ...

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Why are there no forests in Sweden?
Answer: We had to take them out. They were a safety hazard. Luckily, China requires so many chopsticks that we could sell it all off on a single Monday morning. Just kidding. If there’s anything we do have in Sweden, its forest. In fact, the majority of the country is covered in it.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What do you appreciate among the Argentines?
Answer: I’ve met a few Argentinians, and have also visited the country. I have to say I like pretty much everything about them, as well as the country. It’s like an American-sized Italy with mysterious touches of the Andes. If I ever move somewhere else, it is likely Argentina. Having grown up in Europe, with most of my childhood holidays spent in France and Italy and Spain, Argentina feels like a very good blend of these three, in a huge landmass that has everything I have always liked about the southwestern USA, the Alps, the Rocky Mountains, New Zealand, and Norway. It’s a very diverse country in every way, and the bits where I get on famously with the Argentinians are the ones that count: The wine, the food, the music, the cars, the fashion, the style, the architecture, the language. I do make one exception though, as I am bored to tears by soccer, but everything else sits really well with me. I have always experienced the Argentinians as warm, sweet, great looking people who like everything I like, and who live in the same cloud of Eurocentric and Catholic values that have formed me, even though I have since then broken out of that mold. Still, it means that Argentina and its people strike a deeply nostalgic, sentimental chord in me. It’s also a country that has always been homesick for Europe, like me. And it’s a Europe of a metaphysical kind that may never have existed - yet, there we are. I often feel the Argentinians are my people, by default. If I ever get abducted by aliens, and they scan my psyche and whatever there is to be scanned, they’ll probably have their computer come up with the verdict “likely Argentinian”.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What is the nicest big cat?
Answer: A university friend of mine and his father maintained a large kennel for big cats they had rescued from zoos, circuses, and shelters. They had everything - tigers, pumas, lions, panthers, jaguars… but the nicest ones, according to them, were the cheetahs. A cheetah can be just like a house cat. They are gentle, cuddly, affectionate. Except when they run at 140 km/h across the Savannah to bring down a gazelle. Once you get their adrenaline up to that, golly help you. You could say they are big cats with a turbocharger lag. Until you get them going, they are just mellow. Also sweet were, apparently, tigers. Others were somewhere in the middle, and clearly the fiercest and most unpredictable big cats were, according to my friends, the panthers and the jaguars. They really were dangerous and fast like a time lapse. One moment, the cat would be deeply asleep in a corner, and one eye blink later, it was slamming into the bars in front of you, and if it weren’t for them, you’d be so breakfast.

Question: Is Sweden dark in the winter?
Answer: Not entirely, and not all the way through. Yes, winter is when you’ll want some good illumination, in Sweden. The days are short then. Where I live, in Östersund, the sun may come up at 09:00, and be down by 15:00. Further north, you even find some places where the sun won’t come up at all for a few days, but barely anyone lives there. Interestingly, it can feel darker in the south than in the north, because the south usually doesn’t have a permanent snow cover in winter anymore, whereas the north benefits from the reflective qualities of a snow cover that tends to stay put from November till April. Question: What do you think about voice messages?
Answer: I find them a complete waste of time. I’m a great fan of the written word, because it can be consumed silently, at my own pace, and repeatedly in portions if required, allowing for deeper reflection on its individual aspects. A voice message, just like a phone call or a messaging chat, by contrast, is an impertinence. Someone engaging me in one of those is basically saying “you are now my captive until I let you go.” And afterwards, all words have evaporated, potentially with very little echo still lingering. When I get voice messages, I tend to ignore them. Partly because it makes me angry that someone would be so inconsiderate as to just claim my time until they are satisfied, and also because there is simply never a good time, or use, for them. You start playing it, and it disturbs everybody around you, everyone hears what’s being said, including complete strangers, and in the end, you still have no written to do list or record one can work with in silence. One may miss things, or not understand things acoustically, and a good percentage of the time is usually spent blabbing pleasantries and gibberish anyway. I would leave voice messages to the ghosts.

Question: What are some sayings in English that seem strange to non-native speakers?
Answer: When I lived in Nottingham, there was a famous exclamation people sometimes quoted to me, in somewhat conspiratorial spirits, it would seem: “Ay up me duck!” When I first heard it, on a tram, I thought the person saying it wanted me to relinquish my seat to him. I did wonder why he referred to me as a duck, but… when in Rome. And I lived in Nottingham for many years without anyone ever explaining what that saying means. And maybe there is no known explanation for it. But then I came to Stockholm and started using the underground system. That’s where I believe to have found a possible origin for “Ay up me duck” - in the Swedish language, possibly hinting at a Norse connection. As you approach the escalators in the Stockholm metro, coming from a train, those escalators coming down are signposted as “Ej Upp” - literally not up. You see it on the left side in the picture: That’s when it dawned on me that “Ay up” could be the same as “ej upp”, which would then interpret the meaning of “Ay up me duck” to be something like “don’t fly away, my duck!” I’d like that. Very sweet, like saying “don’t go away now, sweetie”. I could see that very much in line with the warm, jovial character of northern England.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What are some English words which mean something else, very different, or funny in other languages?
Answer: One of my favourites is ERRAND. “Running errands” sounds so focused and like we know exactly what we are doing, in English, but I also speak French, and “errand” is a French adjective that describes how someone, or something, moves in an arbitrary and disoriented pattern, perhaps a bit like the Flying Dutchman. Someone who, in French, is “errand” is basically traveling restlessly and without a real destination. And that is what it can feel like to be out there with a car and a shopping list, shuttling from one supermarket to the next, getting who knows what, and forgetting some of it. Such an accidentally fitting term.

Question: Is horror or paranormal known and believed by people in Sweden?
Answer: Today, I took my heart into my hands and drove to Sweden’s most haunted house. The paranormal, in Sweden, has its believers, yes. Many of whom are very intelligent people I know personally, and even work with at university. I can tell by the way some of them react to the topic that they have had experiences that have impressed them deeply. Personally, I had never experienced anything paranormal, and have no special abilities to sense it whatsoever - which, given how many people claim to have it, may well be a special ability in itself. So I took the ghostly white Prius, and embarked on the journey. It’s a bit of a drive, and the last bit of it gets seriously rugged. Eventually, I reached the incredibly scenic village of Borgvattnet, and its Old Vicarage, in Jämtland, northern Sweden. Along the way, the GPS repeatedly told me it had no idea where we were. That’s common here. Luckily, I had a good old paper map. A place that has been on the radar of ghost hunters world wide since 1947, when a journalist spent some time there and recorded what he experienced. Apparently, the place is so infested with ghosts, you pretty much have a guarantee to experience something if you stay long enough. Today, it operates as a café and hotel. Suitably for meeting up with ghosts, I was wearing my white trousers, and made sure I wafted onto the property silently, in electric drive mode. And I had read somewhere that calories and carbohydrates don’t exist when ghosts are around, so I ordered waffles with whipped cream and hjortron jam. A very guilty pleasure for someone on a ketogenic diet, and I hoped to create whatever necessary vortex of guilt may be necessary to see ghosts by doing so. The place did have a strange atmosphere. Despite all the jolly displays that seemed to make light of it, such as merchandise and ghost hunter kits, there was something heavy in the air there. I could feel it, and I am not in any way attuned to the supernatural, remember. It felt like something… stuffy, or sad. The kind of feeling you get when you feel you are about to be choked up by tears. I repeat, I am not into the supernatural, but there was something wrong with that place. This dog kept going crazy: Its owners said “strange, he only ever does that when there are lots of people around…” Really, lots of people? A few cups of coffee later, I began my little tour of exploration of the inside of the house. As a vicarage, it was of course full of religious paraphernalia, quite untypical for modern Sweden. The inside of the house is pretty much original, from the 1940s. A ghost, although it turned out to be made in China: The priest’s old rocking chair, said to start rocking by itself sometimes: I’ll say it again, that place feels weird. Perhaps someone with actual, medial ability would get a lot more out of it in terms of full-on ghost communication than I did, but I was glad to be out in the open again. Where I experienced a strange phenomenon of bubbles in a tub: Perhaps the original inventor of soda fountains is finding no rest. They do have some cool merchandising going there. Say what you want about the Swedes, they have a great sense of humour. You can get a whole ghost hunter kit, plus books, and a two hundred dollar teddy bear - you will appreciate a teddy bear when you’re alone at night in a place like that, I am certain. Talking about using fear to drive up prices. It felt reassuring to see my car again. As I touched the door handle, the central locking suddenly unlocked the entire car. It’s supposed to do that. I was glad no ghost interfered. Laugh all you like, but the thing is that I had tried to drive there the day before with my Pontiac, which promptly broke down along the way. And when I tried to pay for my waffle and coffee, there was a technical failure of the card terminal. Anyway, it felt good to put some distance between me and the place. And the white Prius and I frolicked into the distance, through the wilderness, free from ghosts, feeling lighter and lighter with every mile, and got supernatural gas mileage.
