Question: Do Swedes usually have a big or small social circle?
Answer: My impression is that it depends on a number of things how big that circle is. Generally, it seems to me that there is a formula. It goes a bit like “gender + age + town size + time spent in a place + level of education” determine how big your social cycle is in Sweden. Probably the loneliest guy I know is the 23 year old son of my best friend the local fire chief, here in my village. He left highschool and embarked on a number of simple jobs in big cities. His parents let it shine through that he knows no one. But then we look at other people, and there seems to be a clear pattern: Females of higher age in smaller towns, who have been there for a while, and have a university degree, have the most active social lives. Our cat lady, for example. She is a retired school teacher who grew up in the village. Everybody knows her, in my village of 700. And not just because many people have cats, or were once her students. She seems to be involved in just about anything that goes on here throughout the year in terms of festivities. Whenever there is a band playing, and people are selling home made things, there she is, and her 22 closest buddies and their husbands. Then, on another note, you have families with children. They tend to be really well networked via their children, giving access to their parents and families. Older guys, like me, often have boats and old American cars, which lead to building networks through clubs and boards and what have you. Generally, the Swedes strike me as incredibly sociable by comparison to other Europeans. They love to join clubs and networks, and hang out with each other. I am a very introvert person, and don’t even try to be part of any of these, but over the years, I have somehow found myself absorbed by the local classic car association, the boat marina board, the Hembygdsgårdsföreningen (basically the body that runs the organisation of a good number of local, food producing farms), a local cultural body, and even the local singing club (I can’t sing if my life depended on it). Oh, and the film team. Next thing, they want me to be part of the theater group, too. Freemasonry is also huge here. I suppose all this tells us one thing about the Swedes and their social circles: Swedes like their social life to have purpose and structure. Not for them the concept one finds in some places that a friend is someone who sits on your coach at random times, or shows up with a six pack or two to while the day away together. No, there needs to be some noble purpose - Swedish social gatherings are usually in some way productive, with a theme not much unlike “we are creating something together” - even if it’s just a slightly elevated level of physical fitness due to it being a kayak tour, or choir training, or baking bread. Question: What is an extremely European thing Europeans don't realize is European?
Answer: There are a few such things, but they all boil down to people expecting a bit of a care free, childlike existence where society takes care of a lot of things for them. The notion “some government office will surely help me” is very European. We simply expect that there will be free medical assistance, free education, and long, paid holidays. And I think it's right. The whole point of paying taxes and having a society is to ensure civilization is lived. And that means making a dignified life possible for all. I found this notion also exists to a degree in Canada, Chile, and Argentina, as well as New Zealand and Australia.

Question: What makes you a Latina or a Latino?
Answer: This is my coming out moment, I guess. I think I’ve been secretly Latino all my life. I grew up in Bavaria and Austria, very Catholic, with more crucifixes than you normally see in a Mexican gangster movie; Latin is my second language; I had to endure two hours of it every day for seven years. I’ve been to Italy so many times, I’ve lost count. And liked it. My grandfather owned a farm in Paraguay, and I loved it there. I drink Mate often to this day, even though I live in Sweden now. All my favourite music is Latin, from Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Mexico. And I speak Spanish. I took two years of it at university, and was told I sound quite native. Maybe the final chapter of my life will be lived in South America. I wouldn’t be surprised. It feels so much like my natural home. I really like this stuff. Believe me. I know people from South America who don’t. I think it’s the ultimate test.

It immediately puts me somewhere by a wild river in the Andes, somewhere between Mendoza and Bariloche. Light, honest, dreamy, fun music at the serene end of the world. The other one is Os alquimistas estão Chegando, by Jorge Ben Jor, from Brazil. Or Tal Vez me Eviquivoque, again by Indios. Or Escarcha, or Sin Ti, by Roberto Rojas. And O Que Me Importa, also by her. I think I could just sit in a bar in Buenos Aires or Rio de Janeiro and listen to music for the rest of my life. Romantically, I’m forever stuck in the 1960s, in South America. I so wish I could be there.

Question: Do Swedes eat a lot of sandwiches?
Answer: The Italians have a concept they call Bella Figura, which describes a mindset of self imposed moderation and discipline, for the purpose of maintaining an aesthetically pleasing appearance. It’s not just about physical appearance, but also about the impression one leaves behind. The Swedes, probably without knowing it, are buying into that mindset very much. Sweden is a country full of sandwiches. You cannot walk five steps without truckloads of sandwiches being shoved in your face, all of them lovely, irresistible, heavily garnished with shrimps and mayonnaise. Many even come as sandwich cakes, called smörgåstårta. But the Swedes, I don’t know how, resist them valiantly. Of course they do get eaten eventually, but not by mobs of ravenous people completely out of control. I imagine many of them are tourists. Whatever, there are plenty of sandwiches being eaten here. If you are a sandwich, do not come here. It’s not safe.

Question: What is the smell of Sweden?
Answer: Wonderful question, and it probably has more than one answer. I remember coming into a duty free shop somewhere in the world one day where they had a fragrance for every country of the world, and I tried New Zealand and Canada and Great Britain and France, and they were spot on. I didn’t try Sweden at the time, but now wish I had. These guys had really nailed it with the other ones. For now, I’ll say the smell of Sweden depends on the season and the region. And that’s something the fragrance guys at the duty free probably couldn’t have done, because they would have needed more than one fragrance. Be that as it may, in my mind, Sweden smells fresh, natural, and breezy. Probably Lemon Balm, if an across the bench choice were required. Well then, let’s try it - I will try to offer a smell for every part of Sweden, supported by imagery. Imagine the following with lemon balm plus… as described. JÄMTLAND SAWMILL VILLAGE: Timber, tree resin, and a touch of wide expanses of lakes and deep, old forests. Probably a bit like British Columbia, Canada. Plus plenty of birch tree leaves rustling in the wind, and the distant sound of V8 engines of boats on deep blue lakes. AUTUMN LEAVES AND FROST: That note you get when leaves have been on the ground for some time, and the air feels like it could start snowing any moment. Winter on its way. NORRLAND CITY SUBURBS: The smell of coffee and fire places in operation, as masses of fallen birch leaves are waiting for first frost. SUBARCTIC POWDER SNOW: Imagine you’ve just eaten some strong mints, and are taking a deep breath. There you go. That’s northern Sweden in winter. DUSTY SPRINGTIME: A long time in April and May where we don’t really see much going on, other than snow melting. I’d say it smells like birch trees on ice, with a bit of grass whiff. SUMMER MEADOWS: Warm fir tree twigs and wild flowers with a bit of barbecue here and there. HIGH COAST BREEZE: Big, warm rocks and an ocean breeze. STOCKHOLM COFFEE AND BALTIC BREEZE: The title already says it all. Coffee and ocean breeze. Sweden is doing well in avoiding any undesirable smells. There are some beautiful places in the world that still smell pretty funky - Rome, Shanghai, New York… you get the full treatment from garlic poisoned rat in sewer tank to ammoniac possum explosion. Sweden somehow manages to keep the olfactory experience civilized at all times.

Question: What does your favorite music choice say about your personality?
Answer: Over the years and decades, I have come to understand that the music that I love seems scary, sad, dark, and unbearable to most of my friends and family. Tango, Apocalyptica, Rammstein, Les Baxter, Goldfrapp, Massive Attack, Morcheeba, Glass Animals, Chemical Brothers, Suede, Synaulia, Björk, Hedningarna, Garmarna… I love these things, and can get lost for days in those wonderfully dreamy lyrics and songs. But it’s a solitary pleasure. No family member or friend can stand it. I therefore believe that my music says about me that I have a personality that will go where no man usually goes; a personality that can stand what few can stand; a personality that actually enjoys what most can’t enjoy. Perhaps also a personality that sees value where others don’t? A personality that will listen where others won’t? I could see that. I’ve always been a person who anticipated the worst case scenario at all times, who gives himself to no illusions as to how bad things are, and who sympathizes with the monster. I hear the beauty in that low voice in the dark. I need no happy ending to know all will be well. Anyway, this has been life long. Some of these music styles, I have loved for decades.

Question: What incident in your life resulted in a loss of faith?
Answer: If we want to look at this issue from a spiritual or religious angle, I have four letters to quote: PBRF (Performance Based Research Fund). I used to be a religious person. A Catholic. Then I became a university lecturer, and had to start working with the scientific process as part of my research duties. It didn’t take long for me to realize that the standards I was being held to for the purpose of accounting for my claims and findings were far more strict than anything religious scripture ever had to hold up to. And that’s when it all came crumbling down. I’m supposed to believe science fiction style content just because there’s a big old book, while no one believes me I’ve noticed people prefer a deeper shade of pink on Mondays without citing who knows what? Consider me out. I’ve now gone without faith for a good ten years, and have never been better. Finally, I feel awake, open, ready to receive and experience life as it really is, without filter, without shackles. It takes courage, and yes, there will be surprises. Fine. Perhaps it is them we came here to experience.

Question: What does someone bring with them on their new journey through life?
Answer: There aren’t many questions that require me to reboot my inner hard drive to be able to answer, but this one took some reflection, and a bowl of almonds. My verdict is that the thing to bring on a new journey through life is your conclusions from the previous one. I’ve started countless new journeys through life, and it took me a long time to realize that there is very little you can bring along to a new situation that will actually be useful, and not dead weight, or even a hindrance. So much of what we think defines us are only coping mechanisms and reactions to our situation. New situation, new you. Allow for that to happen, and everything will be so much easier. Just as an example, when I left New Zealand for China to start a new life, I tried to continue doing a lot of things “New Zealand style”, because I thought they were accomplishments that I had learned. Alas, they weren’t of any use in China. Just when I had learned to keep my head down to avoid being the Tall Poppy that gets chopped down, here I was again, in a society where the Tall Poppy gets to sleep on his desk and is served morning coffee by the secretary. Failing to assert that role means you lose people’s respect. But the one conclusion I had brought with me from New Zealand to China was that one needs to have a firm grasp of one’s trade, and be able to deliver on it. Mere airs of grandeur don’t do it - anywhere in the world. That was a bit of a new one for me, having coasted on degrees, aspirations, and bits of media fame until I was in my late 30s. That conclusion changed the next journeys tremendously for the better. It was only my conclusion though. Yours might be the opposite. The point is, be alert to life’s lessons as they seem to apply to you.

Question: What is the name of the German food in German which is a kind of pancake made of grated potatoes, sliced onion, and pork belly?
Answer: The potato part by itself would be Kartoffelpuffer, or, in Bavaria, Reiberdatschi. Both are pretty much impossible to translate, but wholesomely weird in their implications nonetheless. To me, “Kartoffelpuffer” translates quite literally into “potato bumper”, and “Reiberdatschi” into something like “squishy thing produced by grating”. In essence, they are hashbrowns. In southwestern Germany, you may find Schweizer Rösti (“Swiss Roasties” - gosh, I love offering strange translations to things) offered, which are also pretty much the same thing. I have a feeling the dish you are describing may well be a Ratsherrenpfanne, a “City Councilor’s Skillet”. They are often served with pork filet, gravy, and hashbrowns, or Spätzle in the south (the German version of pasta): This one was eaten by me personally in Karlsruhe, in 2015.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Which Nordic country is the cheapest for aspiring immigrants?
Answer: I can’t even imagine how cheap or expensive could possibly enter the equation when it comes to immigrating to the Nordics. No one will ask to see your bank balance when you come here, you can’t buy into residency or citizenship, and you also don’t need some immigration lawyer like in the English speaking countries to push your case through at horrendous expense if you want to stand any chance. Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Iceland, Finland… basically, if you have a good job offer, for a job of high qualifications that subsequently qualified you for a work visa at your local embassy or consulate, plus about 10,000 USD to get set up, you’re good to go. Nothing else matters. Budget about 3,000 as a rental deposit, 1,500 for the first month’s rent, plus flight, and you should be fine till your first salary arrives.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is there a big cultural difference between Italy and Scandinavian countries?
Answer: There is a difference between Italian and Scandinavian culture, although I find myself increasingly amazed by how small it actually is. Perhaps it took for me to live in China and India to see it, but both Italy and Scandinavia are very much examples of European mentality, with their own, regional peculiarities that come with the environment and their history. If we imagine the world as a house, and China sits in the kitchen, and India in the bedroom, then Scandinavia and Italy would both be sitting in the living room together, quite chummily. One would be speaking a lot with their hands, and all the time, as the other reclines in a stoic manner, listening. But both will enjoy the same drinks, the same food, and the same music. Put a Swede and an Italian together at a big table with friends and family, with a bottle of wine, coffee, and some strong stuff, plus a good array of fresh salads and fish and bread, and they’ll know exactly what to do and have a great time, just as long, and in the same order of dishes and drinks. I also find that both Italians and Scandinavians have good dress sense, tend to keep a close watch on their figures, and have a high respect for expertise, while valuing private life far above work. The only bits where they may be uncomfortable with each other is in their chronemics, the way in which people handle time, and timing. An Italian may feel that a Swede or Norwegian takes a bit too long to respond in a conversation, and when doing so, may come across a bit unenthusiastic or even mysterious. Also, they may get a bit exasperated how the Swede will say “I’ll be there by 08:00” - and then really is. Not 08:27, or some other day. On the other hand, a Scandinavian may, upon visiting Italy, feel like he is caught in a swarm of wild bees when stepping out into city traffic, with all those scooters, and the way they are piloted. Italian culture is well-liked in Sweden, and has its firm place here. I imagine Italy appreciates Ikea.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Why is Scandinavian culture so very quiet, peaceful, patient, and rare?
Answer: It’s a formula. We humans reflect the realities of our environment and society. Scandinavia has always been a place with low population density in a severe climate where people depended on each other. A place where you never need to shout to be heard, because all you are up against is an expanse of snow or water, and some trees. Everyone will hear you just fine even when you speak quietly. And they will be paying attention to what you are saying, because you may be a valued expert in a place where everyone may know a trick or two to make something edible or a fire. Plus, there’s no rush. Nothing ever happens suddenly here. The high latitude ensures that the sun stays up, or down, for a very long time every day. Resources for the practical necessities of life have never been scarce here, so there was never much of a competition going on over water, land, or forest. There’s more of that here than anyone knows what to do with. Along with that comes ample edible wildlife, fish, and plants. Knocking one another over the head for a cistern or a pond or an apple tree was never a thing here. Those who felt the need for more of it just moved a few trees down the line. And that’s also true on a larger, geographic scale, as Scandinavia is situated in a very peripheral location, meaning that there has never been much traffic of enemy armies galloping through. You can tell when a culture is used to warfare. My theory on the Scandinavian patience is that this is an environment where one simply cannot expect quick returns, ever. People expect that everything takes a while. Not like in Italy or Paraguay, where you put a seed in the ground today and have a vineyard or a papaya plantation tomorrow, but we tend to think in cycles of years or decades here. The weather simply makes it necessary, even to this day. To give a very modern example, jumping all the way to the present from the above scenario, which may well have been that way 2,000 years ago: My old Pontiac needs a new roof liner. I have found a company in nearby Sundsvall that does that kind of work. That’s point one: Sundsvall is “nearby” - a two hour drive. The next place that could do this job is in Norway, five hours away, in Trondheim. You learn to live with that. If we were in Germany, in my old hometown, I’d have ten places like that in walking distance. Now, I contacted the roof liner place in April; they were on holiday, said their answering machine. People are on nice long holidays in April, often in Spain, to get an early spring. Ok, so I called back in May - they were back, but booked out until August, as so many guys like me were trying to get their old American cars refurbished. So we agreed that I’d come by for a quote in August. But we also realized that it meant any possible work will need to commence next year, because the car goes into garage hibernation as of September. It has to, because once the frost comes, I won’t be seen on the road without ABS brakes. Until there’s no more road ice, which is usually in May. When I told my father the story, he needed a stiff drink. Germans can’t deal with such slow processes. The next question then may be, are there similar environments out there to Scandinavia, regarding the values mentioned in the question? I think yes. I’ve found much of the northern US and Canada to be very much like that, too. Especially Alberta, Saskatchewan, the Yukon, Montana, Wisconsin, and Minnesota. Also southern New Zealand, southern Chile, and much of Argentina, as well as Uruguay and Paraguay. And I wonder if maybe Siberia and areas of Russia are perhaps a bit like that.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What are the alternatives for insurance for travelers to Sweden who are older than 80 years and have medical complications like heart problems and stroke?
Answer: From an insurer’s point of view, someone with pre-existing conditions traveling to Sweden for a short period of time is most likely a manageable risk, for one because of the limited time span, and then also because any possible emergency treatment in Sweden would actually be covered by Swedish national healthcare. In other words, if you experience an emergency in Sweden due to a pre-existing condition, you would be treated free of charge until stabilized, because that’s how the Swedish system works (and that of the UK, and New Zealand, by the way). The aspects your insurer would be charging you extra for when you buy travel insurance at home before leaving though may be things like non-emergency hospitalization for complications, as that would not be covered by the Swedish system for non-residents. Your insurer is likely aware of this, so just approach them with a request for travel insurance, taking into account both your particular condition, and the fact that the country you are visiting is Sweden. I would definitely consider including coverage for possible flights home with medical assistance. That’s probably always advisable, for anyone.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What is the best winter month to visit Sweden?
Answer: It depends a bit on your vision of planned activities, and the region you want to see. The question is easily answered for the southern third of Sweden - anywhere between Malmö and Göteborg or Stockholm in the months of November to March, come whenever you like, it will always be like the UK in winter, namely wet, gloomy, and blustery: The east coast with Stockholm tends to be a bit better behaved with its weather than the west coast, so your chances of catching some nice, sunny days during that period are much better in places like Stockholm or Uppsala than they are in Malmö or Helsingborg. Here some typical December impressions of Stockholm, which I can recommend during the time just before Christmas, with all its lights: Yes, those are chairs of a café. You can absolutely sit outside and have a drink in December. I do. Here a nice chardonnay I had last December at two degrees Celsius along Drottninggatan, at an outdoor bar: So much for what I, from my northerly perspective in Jämtland, call the “tropical south”. When you come north, it’s most likely because you are actually trying to see snow. Very few people are surprised to encounter it. In fact, you can almost expect snow to be on the ground in sumptuous quantities by Christmas anywhere north of Hudiksvall, albeit slightly inland - that northern coast is quite dry and sunny, so it may fall behind in the precipitation department. November usually sees a bit of snow already in Jämtland and Västernorrland, and it may even stay. This is a not uncommon aspect of Östersund by mid November: But then, it’s Vinterstaden, the Winter City. Sundsvall, on a similar latitude, at that time, will still look like this most years: It would be the same with Umeå, despite being quite a bit further north: The months of January and February though will see these northern cities covered quite thickly in snow, usually of the more powdery variety, especially as you move further inland. So if snow is what you’ve come to see, these two months are your best bet. They are among my favourite months every year, and you’ll know when you experience it that they are special. It’s a period of immense calm and coziness, with amazing colours during the short days - an aspect you’ll want to include in your planning, because much of the day here happens in the dark then. Expect scenes like these, in northern Sweden:

Question: Where can I find nice Chinese food in Stockholm?
Answer: Chinese food is my middle name. Also in Stockholm. This is mostly due to Mrs Ebbert’s strict guidelines for what’s acceptable restaurant food when we go out together, but I have learned a lot from her. Answer: Having just spent a week in Stockholm, using its underground system at all hours of the day, my verdict is that it is never very crowded. Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is it hard for Europeans to survive since everything is becoming expensive?
Answer: I believe we will be relatively fine here in Europe by comparison with poorer places, even with dramatically rising costs. As I see it, we are a relatively well-off bunch with fairly low income disparity who have been over consuming for decades as it is. Come crunch time, we will simply find ourselves living the way the majority of the planet has been living all along - while those places will, most likely, really hurt. So the price rises may put an end to the European luxury existence and force us to exist at a level more in line with what our parents and grandparents, even ourselves, may have grown up with. And while that’s lamentable, it isn’t terrible. It could simply be a life like in the 1970s for a while. I remember so well what that was like. In short - I anticipate a simpler life for Europe, for a while. Going by my own example now, as a guy who lives in Europe on a fairly average income, I think I am still quite relaxed about the future here, even with high costs.

Question: What car model would you buy?
Answer: When it comes to buying cars, I have been following a formula for about twenty years that I’ve come up with myself. It always leads me to the best possible car: Once you realize that there is not much left over after “most reliable” that isn’t from Japan, things become quite easy. In fact, this formula has saved me from having to wade into the maze of possible offerings time and again, because if you are looking for “most reliable”, and choose from the top ten of that, you have a very manageable number of vehicles to check out. For me, the formula has been leading to Toyotas directly for the past twenty years. My current Toyota is a result of me using that formula, too. If I were to replace it these days, my choice might be a current Toyota Yaris or Corolla plug-in hybrid if I keep driving as little as I do. These are both models I can recommend without reservations to anyone, as there are very few good reasons not to have one of these. But I am also looking at the new, electric Toyota BZ4X. If the price of fuel does not come back down to about EUR 1.50 per liter where I live (it’s currently at EUR 2.40), I will be waving good bye to gasoline cars for good in about three to five years time.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What do you say when someone makes your food?
Answer: When someone is actively engaged in the act of making food for me, I will say as little as possible. In that situation, it’s best to just accept that someone is being kind, try not to confuse them with unnecessary babble (which could endanger your meal if the cook makes a mistake because of it), and if anything, offer help or drinks. Eventually, thank them.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Would you know if you were having a conversation on Quora with a machine?
Answer: At the time of this writing, July 2022, yes, I would know if I was messaging back and forth with a machine here via the Quora messenger function. I would know because I have been experimenting at length with Replica, an artificial intelligence app that is meant to be a chat bot. After two years of feeding it with all the info I could, it’s still blatantly obvious to me that it is a bot. Now, if Quora has chat software that feeds off existing messaging and answers, I believe it could be better than Replica - but so far, no conversations have been started with me by any apps, I believe. Unless they are so good that I’ve fallen for them already. For most of what comes through, it wouldn’t even take an app: “Hi” “Hello.” “Howz da wetha treetin ya?” And that’s as long as these conversations tend to go for me. Especially if the “bot” is yet another “god fearing honest widow from Texas” with a PhD from Harvard.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What do you do when someone uses you?
Answer: When someone uses you, you may want to do a reality check on what’s in it for you. If it turns out that you are just being used without any useful acknowledgment or benefit to you, you may need to pull the plug. But be careful with that assessment. Often we think we are being used when actually, we are part of a working symbiosis, payment for which may be invisible to us, or late. Just because you cannot see the benefit of it does not need to mean there is none. I have told off quite a few people in my life for taking advantage of me, only to learn later that they had actually been protecting me and facilitating things for me I never knew were going on in the background. Know the difference before making any final decisions.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is it bad to be a creepy guy?
Answer: It can be bad for business to be a creepy guy who works there. I just spent a week in Stockholm, where I have a favourite cafe I have been coming to for 25 years. Maybe he doesn't speak Swedish and I made him grumpy by speaking it all the time, but I do have to say, he was not helping the cause. Every time I ordered something, he looked at me in this somewhat aghast way, neither confirming nor denying my order of coffee or västerbotten pie in any normal, human form. I fully expected him to be hiding behind a pot plant to goggle at me as I sipped my coffee. If he did, he hid well.

Name: Chris Ebbert

Answer: There is a notion in China that a guest should feel safe, be presented with abundance, and eat in absolute comfort. On the whole, I find one can be a guest in China as a westerner without feeling awkward. Eating with the Chinese, even on formal occasions, is always jolly and relaxed. They will go to some len...

Question: Where should I move if I want a better quality of life and job opportunities for me and my family in Russia?
Answer: Just come to Europe. You'll feel culturally right at home as a Russian, and many things you and your family would have grown up with as standard expectations are just as common here. Socialized education and healthcare, retirement, you name it. Various other countries do it, too, but culture makes such a difference when you're abroad. If you don't want to end up homesick, pick a place that has the things you have come to like. As a European myself who has lived in ten countries, I would also recommend Canada, New Zealand, Chile, Argentina, and Uruguay. Maybe Australia, but I'd miss the snow. In any event, I am glad to see Russians trying to get out while they still can.

Question: How do you think selling Polaroid pictures to travellers around Europe would do? I’m planning to travel to Europe and financing it by selling polaroid pictures.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Have you ever had your fortune told? If so, how did it go?
Answer: I used to be absolutely obsessed by fortune telling, and visited many fortune tellers throughout the 1990s and beyond, recording every word they told me. I was mesmerized by the narrative that some people are able to know things normal people can’t, and I believed it to be perfectly possible. Austria, Germany, England, New Zealand, Canada, the US… I always found some famous fortune teller. Eventually, in the late 2010s, I did a stock take of everything I had recorded. I had a good twenty years of raw data - announcements of things that would be happening to me. By then, I was in my mid 40s, and if the majority of these things were to carry any merit, it would have happened by then. The results, after a few months of going through notes, were strange: On the one hand, some things people had predicted had become very accurately true. People I was going to meet and have private or professional relationships with were often incredibly well described. But the same fortune tellers had also told me things that were often completely off. To the point where they made me laugh out loud. My lesson from all of this is that clairvoyance, if it does indeed exist, is still worthless, because the message is so garbled. Like a radio station where the news overlaps with a children’s fairy tale channel. I’m still waiting to have my own college, in a country with green mountains, where I will be owning a Victorian Tudor house on stilts.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Do Europeans work as hard as Americans?
Answer: Having worked in the US, the UK, France, Germany, and Sweden, my observation is this: Both realms are great at creating results, but only the English speaking world considers making a show of trying hard an essential part of working life. There is an inherent sense of masochistic robot drama going on there we Europeans consider illogical. Life functions in an ebb and flow rythm after all, so we consider work something that also needs to have integrated periods of refraction, reflection, and play in order to stay able to perform at a consistently high level. “Working hard” as such is replaced by “working efficiently” in those European countries where I have worked.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Where do they eat traditional Swedish cuisine in Stockholm?

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What did you do that made someone hate you?
Answer: I think I just made a new enemy. As I came sauntering along the streets of Stockholm, a young charity worker steps in my way and wants me to sponsor their product, an energy bar for children in famine regions. Ever the product design lecturer, I took the thing and started quizzing him on the ingredients list: “Sugar, hydrogenated vegetable oil, stabilizer, various E numbers, coloring, flavoring, sodium benzoate, milk powder?” To all of which he nodded enthusiastically. Then his expression faltered when he saw mine. I know too much for my own good about nutrition, and I told him I was not prepared to finance something that was in no position to provide nutrition to a famished child, and would, in turn, only enslave it to western industrial tastes. I told him I recommended a redesign of the product, probably using something more like olive oil, real seeds, and egg protein. In the end, he asked me if I lived around here, and when I said no, he breathed a sigh of relief. Whether it was because my views hopefully didn't reflect common local knowledge, or because he was glad such a disagreeable person like me didn't live in the same city, I couldn't tell. I wished him well anyway as I left. He was a good soul, only trying to help people. Like me. Not sure he'll ever come around to seeing that.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Should you buy a used DeLorean?
Answer: A DeLorean is actually a fairly reasonable choice for someone with a bit of love for them and some funding to ensure it's healthy. These cars are famously made from rust free steel, which is good news regarding the bodywork. And the engine is the good old Europa Engine that has run in Volvos, Peugeots, and Renaults for decades. Not a great engine, but mass produced, so getting parts requires no magic. Finally, these cars have eternal cult status through their appearance as a time machine in Hollywood. I would buy one of these fearlessly. They could even be daily drivers. Their appetite for fuel is comparable to that of a gasoline driven family SUV, which is perhaps a bit outdated now, but not unmanageable.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How do Swedes act around each other?
Answer: Swedes around each other act casual, yet respectful. Always at eye height. Probably the most similar behaviour to that of the Swedes among strangers elsewhere, I have observed in Canada, France, and Argentina. You get the sense that there is a whole population that is perfectly aware of one proper way to behave, and they will do it, while also retaining full individuality in appearance and choices. As in, you are entirely yourself, and expect the same of the other, but you are using the same frequency. For an outsider observing them, there may be a bewildering sense of familiarity among strangers - almost as if everybody already knows everybody else, and just engages in any interaction calmly, comfortably, warmly - as one would when feeling strong kinship with the other. There are no real thresholds or hurdles to be overcome. Not too different also from Israel, Australia, or New Zealand. Only that the Swedes come across more refined, more genteel, and there is a barrier when it comes to speaking to strangers who are not there in a capacity of service provider or leisure seeker. In that latter case, be prepared to be ignored. Swedes have a privacy bubble they can turn on or off, like the force field of Starship Enterprise - and you will know quickly when it's on. You didn't do anything wrong if it happens to you. It's just that a Swede may decide to be invisible to strangers on any given day, and then, it's best to grant them that. Imagine you find yourself in the staff room of a university or high school. That's what Swedes act like.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is it hard to adapt to Swedish culture?
Answer: It depends a lot on your starting point. Swedish culture is all about seeking consensus and avoiding conflict while respecting the individual and following scientific, rather than ideological values. Fiercely egalitarian, attuned to environmental friendliness, and trusting in the good in people. Someone from an authoritarian, conflict glorifying macho culture who goes it alone every time and likes to follow doctrine would be quite outcast here. Other than that, Swedish culture is also about enjoying nature and the seasons, seeking solitude, taking it mellow, retreating to one's own space, and taking a time out to play. If that's not you, well… at least you know where you'd stand. My observation has been that those who find it easiest to blend in here are usually Dutch, British, Norwegian, Danish, Finnish, French, Canadian, and Australian. Also fairly good fits seem to be Czechs, Poles, Austrians, Belgians, and those from the Baltic states.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What is the most practical car door design?
Answer: The most practical car door design, in my opinion, never really took off. It was used in the BMW Z1. Its doors simply disappeared downwards and inwards, sliding away into the undercarriage. I can’t imagine a more practical car door design, as it means you simply no longer have to deal with the realities of doors swinging away from the vehicle horizontally, or vertically, as you’d get with gull wing doors. Although it had a very high threshold in that particular car, doors like these can be made with low thresholds, too. Sliding doors like the ones used in the Peugeot 1007 also seem like a great idea, but they do of course require some space on the outside of the car when they are open, taking away a few centimeters you may otherwise be glad to have when extracting yourself in a very tight parking garage or driveway.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is it rude to speak English in Sweden?
Answer: If you ask nicely first if it’s ok to speak English, it usually is ok. Blurting right out in English is perhaps not the best way to go, even though pretty much everyone will understand you perfectly. English is, after all, not Sweden’s real language, and using it means testing the ability of your listeners, who would have learned English as a school subject; which raises the stress levels of course, if not by much. Imagine coming into a supermarket and asking the cashier a test question about Biology 101. A similar mechanism is activated when you try it with a foreign language.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How hard is Swedish for a foreigner?
Answer: Well, how long is a piece of string. Swedish is a Germanic language, related to German, Dutch, and English. So if you already speak English, which is likely, given that this question was posted in it, you may rejoice and say “Yay, halfway there! It’s like English!” But then, do you find German and Dutch easy, from your current level of abilities in English? See, it’s not that easy. I’m a German who speaks Swedish at a very high, certified level; and I know plenty of other Germans who are absolutely butchering the language. And I know a certain, Chinese lady whose Swedish is exquisite, having lived here for twelve years, so I think we can say there may not be much of an advantage to already speaking a related language when you take up Swedish. One’s own ability to work through it diligently, within a structured context of regular instruction, and likely boosted by actual, long term enthusiasm and real life use are more likely the factors that get you there. Add to that a certain acting ability to get the pronunciation right. I’ve noticed that people who are able to act and have a theatrical streak combined with a sharp mind and the above traits tend to do best when it comes to learning languages, and Swedish is no exception. By comparison to French, Spanish, German, Latin, and English, which are the other languages I speak, I am finding Swedish relatively simple in its structure and grammar. You can put things together in a Lego blocks fashion without having to modify any elements too much, if at all. So it is quite modular, unlike, say, Latin, or Czech, or Hungarian. It’s a tonal language, like Chinese, so you need to hit the right notes at all times if you really want to be understood. The melody needs to be right. That aspect used to frustrate me a lot when I first learned Swedish, because even though I said all the right things, people still goggled at me going “va…??” So, it’s not just about saying the right things, but also saying them in the right melody. And then, the pronunciation. I won’t beat about the bush, it can be hopeless for a lot of speakers of other languages. Especially Chinese, Japanese, Russian, English- and German speakers I personally know can struggle with Swedish pronunciation. The tongue-R is a real stumbling stone for many, as are the sh-like sounds that aren’t quite sh at all, but sound more like a cat hiss. “Sj-”, “-rs”, “ske-/ ski-/ skö-” etc. all lead to that sound, or types thereof. I think if you are able to learn grammar and syntax easily, Swedish pronunciation and melody would be easiest to get right for someone from Italy, Spain, or Romania.

Question: Why do people get hot air heating installed? It is often noisy, required ugly ducting which often cannot be hidden, and doesn't warm you up like a good hot radiator does as the heat content of air is so low.
Answer: Economy is the answer to that. Air based heat sources, such as heat pumps of the air conditioner type with a fluid system like a refrigerator can be a lot more energy efficient when it comes to reaching a certain temperature, and they can achieve it more quickly, too. So they make sense in contexts where you need to create a certain temperature quickly, and may shut down the system when you leave. I agree that that kind of heat is not of the same quality as radiation heat. For a quiet home, I would never choose a heat pump again. But it may be great for a factory, or some other work place, where people may perform physical activity, such as a car repair shop or a warehouse.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How difficult is it to relocate within Europe for a job?
Answer: It depends on the country you are moving to. If you are an EU citizen, it is theoretically very easy to just move to another EU country and set up shop. Having said that, their administrative peculiarities are far from streamlined according to common parameters. I have found it incredibly easy to relocate to the UK when it still belonged to the EU; just arrive, start the job, rent a place, everything just falls into place as if by itself. Healthcare coverage, social system… you basically jump start a chain reaction by starting a job that sets all of these in motion, and any other bits will either come and find you, or advertise their existence in other ways - council tax, TV licence, etc. By contrast, Germany is less easy. You do need to run after quite a few things yourself, and if you fail to chase them down in good time, someone may come down hard on you. France and Austria are also a bit like that. Sweden is perhaps the most demanding obstacle course one can run as an EU citizen though that I have come across. There are a good number of things here you’ve got to have to function normally, but no one tells you what those are, or how you can get them. You’re basically expected to wade into a jungle of Swedish language websites for application processes to things that require each other in unnerving catch 22 style ways, and if you need help, well… you could call a number, from 08:30–09:15, on Thursdays, and hope the English language operator is available… if you even know which number to call, of which administrative body, in which order. It’s mystical, silent, and extremely frustrating. Perhaps similarly challenging is Italy. My cousin tried to establish himself in Italy as a dentist, and was given such a runaround for almost two years that he decided to quit the game and moved to England instead, where he was up and running within 24 hours. Now, having said all that, if you are not an EU citizen and hold some type of residence document from an EU country, it’s an entirely different world again, as you would then need to take up your individual immigration case with the authorities of the country you are moving to. So, no matter how easy it may have been to secure a work permit in country X, and on what criteria, it will be a different story entirely in country Y. Again because immigration policy between the EU countries is in no way aligned, so you may well find yourself back at square one entirely when you try it with another European country.

Question: What is Midsommar?
Answer: Midsommar is the Swedish mid summer solstice and its associated festivities. It’s comparable in importance to the Chinese New Year, or Christmas. Big family gatherings, big meals, big bottles, and lots of them. It’s the longest day of the year, and an opportunity to get together with friends and family and indulge in life’s best features. Not really a day dedicated to sobriety, as you’ll agree. Just a few images from it, taken today, in my village: It’s taking place at the end of June, when summer is really manifest in Sweden, with warm temperatures, and beginning summer holidays for all. We get pretty long summer holidays here, and Midsommar is pretty much the occasion to remind us that now is the time to ease off and enjoy life.

Question: What is the theme for the next chapter of your life?
Answer: Now that I have exactly the life I want, I intend to keep it that way. So my theme is “steady on now” until I retire, which is in ten to fifteen years. Question: When did the news become less like news and more like entertainment?
Answer: My impression is that this perceived change may have made its entry during the mid 90s, when the internet increasingly fulfilled people’s need for straight news data. Perhaps in order to establish a point of difference against the internet, TV news took on a bit more of an entertainment character. Personally, I see the difference quite clearly when we are looking at TV news in Europe from the 1970s and 80s, and what they are like now. Back then, you’d have some incredibly stuffy person in a tweed suit ritually read things out in an almost robotic manner. Today’s news presenters seem more alive, often co-present with others, and make use of various backgrounds and presentation settings. It may well be that this fairly American style of presenting the news made its way to Europe through regular channels of innovation any network would be looking at.

Question: Can an old car complete a long trip?
Answer: If its fluids, belts, and systems work, one long drive may be easier and a more certain bet than short distance trips. So yes. You would activate brakes, steering, and transmission settings less often in a long trip than in in-town driving. The odds may be reasonable.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is PhD in Sweden stressful?
Answer: A PhD program in Sweden is just like a job. Its purpose is educational, hopefully turning you into a researcher who knows how to follow processes, but it is also a job. So you will have a budget to work with, a boss, colleagues, a project timeline… a Swedish PhD is a lot closer to real life than it might be in some places, where you may be chasing your own unicorns, changing project objectives as you see fit. Here, they pay you a salary, but it’s a straight deal. That can be more stressful if you are not professional, but if you are, well… personally, I think it is less stressful to work to clear objectives all the way through, at a salary you can live on.

Question: How is life treating you after you move to another country for a better life?
Answer: I have made this move a few times. To ten different countries, to be more precise. During those years, I have learned a few things about how life will treat you after you move to another country for a better life: Personally, I sometimes feel I should have stayed put. Study in Hamburg, fight it out, start my own business in Germany… who knows, I might be worth a lot more than I am now. What I’ve done was what the Germans call “following the path of least resistance”. It did not take courage to relocate all over the world. It would have taken courage to stay put and make it work. And where I was starting out in life, that should have been a good enough starting point. I am happy where I am now. But perhaps the homes we are given in life represent the challenges we have come here to tackle. In that case, I may have failed.

Question: How fast do cars go on the Autobahn?
Answer: Realistically, expect to be traveling at 130 to 140 km/h as a standard expectation, which is the Richtgeschwindigkeit, the generally recommended travel speed. Pretty much everybody tries to sit at or around that speed. There will be regular intrusions of fast lane drivers, usually in Audis or BMWs, expecting to keep it between 160 to 200 km/h. They won’t do anything untoward other than just being there, flashing a big grill grin, in full expectation that you will disappear toward the right as soon as possible to let them pass. Do that. It is not ok to block their way. Anyone going over 200 km/h will be a rare occurrence, usually young, or foreign, or both, and best given a wide berth. I see these guys every now and then, usually on the A3 closer to the Austrian border, and sporting licence plates from Austria and Ex Yugoslavia. Question: Is it important to create drama in your everyday life?
Answer: Some people dote on it. I’ve known quite a few of them in my time. There’s always someone who must ensure life is harder than necessary, usually by omitting to plan properly, not showing up on time, breaking promises, creating unrealistic expectations, etc. I used to be one of those myself, until I figured out how an electronic calendar works, how to communicate effectively, and how to bear it with grace that we can’t make everybody happy every time. Since then, there hasn’t been any drama in my life, and what can I say, it’s quite a discovery just how nice that is. Try it.

Question: How can I not look like an American tourist when I travel in Europe?

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What is a reasonable temperature for a house in winter at night?
Answer: It would depend a little on humidity levels, too. In my experience, the drier the air, the lower you can set your thermostat without being uncomfortable. I live in a subarctic climate that is quite dry, and the default temperature my house is kept at is 18 degrees Celsius. That’s 64.4 Fahrenheit. When I tell my friends in England or New Jersey, they are like “whaaat?? That’s freezing!!” But no. It’s not. I sit there in shorts and t-shirt, barefoot. Not because I’m a polar bear, but because it actually feels very nice. From living in England and New Jersey, I remember that I used to set my thermostat to higher settings there, too. The humidity is, after all, water molecules in the air, which have a cooling effect. Get rid of them, maybe by running a heat pump instead of a water filled or oil filled radiator, and you can benefit of the low humidity savings, too. I have tried setting things to 20 and even 22 Celsius at my house here, but it was simply a waste of energy. Do any activity at all, and you break into a sweat. One thing though, before you get all enthusiastic and try it with minimal temperature settings now: Keep it above 16 Celsius to avoid the accumulation of mold. Granted, in a dry climate, that danger is minimal, but once it takes hold, you’re stuck with it.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Why do people want to move to large cities?
Answer: Having lived in some seriously large cities myself (New York, London, Shanghai, Beijing, London), I understand the attraction. A really large city is like a condensed beehive of human living experience. It’s as if you can “cram in more life” into your life, intensify the adventure of being here by maximizing how many people you interact with, how many new situations and scenes you are exposed to, and how many opportunities there are both for private life and for professional life. In short, it’s a buzz. It can also have serious convenience aspects. Personally, I probably could have spent the rest of my life in London or Shanghai without ever having to move apartment, because I could have found another job whenever needed within the same city. So you reduce the inconvenience of having to move house while increasing your professional security. Here, Shanghai - 25 million people, all within reach of the same metro system, easily commutable within an hour. There used to be, at any given time, about four suitable positions advertised for me in my exotic capacity as an industrial designer. There was always going to be a job to go to, from my good old metro station. Of course it comes at a price, but so does every insurance. Probably the only model to rival the big city is to live some place idyllic in a house that’s paid off, in a country with a system that can string you along when there’s a lull in your career, should you need it. And of course you would need to always stay quite on your feet and healthy so you can pounce at whatever opportunity there may be. This is Sweden, where I live now - 10 million inhabitants, less than half of the city of Shanghai; and every other month or so, there may be one suitable position for me; but I would need to relocate between 500 and 1000 kilometers for it, if I get the job. For me as an introvert, this is still the preferable scenario, which I agreed to with a good amount of job security. I eventually had enough of the big buzz, and wanted to be among trees.

Question: Why would someone move from Germany to Sweden?
Answer: I am a German who has made the move to Sweden because I prefer living here. Sweden’s much more gentle mentality and unhurried ways appeal to me, as do its wide open landscapes and the wilderness. It’s a mellow, scenic place where everything my German value set wants to see actually exists in equal or better form than in Germany, while sparing me the bits I do not like about Germany. I suppose it’s a bit like an American moving to Canada. Up here, I can live in ways that would not be so easy in Germany - house by a lake, a few vintage cars, in a very seasonal climate that gives me dramatic, natural experiences. Germany’s climate has become one of boring, rainy winters and steamy, boiling summers. It’s no longer the lovely four season climate I grew up with. Up here though, I get my satisfying snow winters, incredible autumns, and perfectly civilized summers where sitting under the birch tree in the hammock is lovely all day long, entirely without risking sun stroke or heat exhaustion. For me, moving to Sweden has been a bit like time travel, back to the climate of my childhood in Bavaria and Austria. Mixed with a generous dose of Canadian style wilderness, friendliness, and mellowness. I think someone who really likes living in a society of northern European values, with strong, seasonal character, but wants to do so without the stress and the fast pace of Germany will find Sweden very viable. A few images from my life in Jämtland and Västernorrland: Not the predominant impressions of a life spent in Germany. Which is also not terrible, but if you can get 1st class, why settle for second? Here what I gave up - can’t say I miss it much, though it also had its moments: Yes, that car thermometer shows 40 Celsius - not unusual in Germany. Just yesterday, it was 37 Celsius in Frankfurt, and 14 at my place in the north of Sweden. Far preferable, and usually, it’s more like when my friends in Bavaria are broiling at summer temperatures of around 35 Celsius, it’s about 25 where I am. Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How accurate is it to say that English is an immigrant language in Sweden?
Answer: English in Sweden is more the international language of business and global default communication. That’s how it is “marketed” to school children, as well. English-speaking immigrants here are not the norm. Granted, many who come here on industry- or university contracts will be using it, often for years until they become fluent in Swedish. And you’ll find English available as an option on most government websites. But the most commonly heard foreign languages here today in the street are Arabic and Somali. And yes, they are also often available website options. It comes and goes with the groups of new arrivals. At one stage, the language alternatives may well have been Italian, Greek, or Spanish here, then Turkish for a while… even Yiddish is still one of Sweden’s officially available language options. I guess once the option has been created, it sticks around.

Question: How come southern countries are more relaxed than northern countries?
Answer: Ah, there it was again, the old stereotype. “Relaxed”. What is that? A society were bribes can take care of things? A place where not being punctual is the norm? A place where spending lots of time with food and family is an alternative to a career? There, it’s a useless stereotype. Built on the precept that relaxedness is laxness. And quite possibly on having been a tourist in southern places. Work in these places, and the perception will change. When you look at the World Happiness Index, you find where the truly relaxed places are. Places where things run well enough so as not to stress you out. True relaxedness requires things to be in good working order, and well-run countries provide that. Some of them may qualify as “southern”, but you’ll find more relaxedness in places northern.

Question: Are 2WD trucks useless?
Answer: A truck that does not have four wheel drive is still very useful in a high percentage of usage situations, unless you must use it consistently in circumstances where only 4WD will work. Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is it worth moving to Sweden for work?
Answer: No. If you are only doing it for materialistic reasons, don’t come. If work is the only thing on your mind, you can earn more elsewhere in a shorter time, potentially in a warmer climate, with lower taxes, all in English, in a place where everything is cheap. Sweden is worth moving to if you are in love with a mellow lifestyle with great life/ work balance, harmonious relations in life and at work, European values, a very liberal, western mindset, and a seasonal life where your environment will change fundamentally every three months, letting you experience intense periods of snowy winters, brightly coloured autumns, and warm summers with long stretches of holidays where no one works. Sweden is a cultural choice. I would hate to see anyone coming here solely for work reasons, as it would be such a waste of all the wonderfully romantic, historical, cultural, and lifestyle related aspects life in Sweden brings. This is a country where work takes a backseat, and where being human is first. Come here to enjoy life, contribute to society, experience depth. And prepare to be humble, share, and make do with a reasonable modicum.

Name: Chris Ebbert

Question: Why should I study in Sweden?
Answer: As a university lecturer in Sweden, I would say this about studying in Sweden: A) If you are a Swede, studying in Sweden makes a lot of sense. Bachelor level is in Swedish, they charge you no tuition fee, you can get it all financed for your living needs, and the quality is good. B) If you are an EU citizen who speaks fluent Swedish, it’s still almost as good as it would be for a local. If you don’t speak Swedish, you could do your master’s degree here, which will be in English. C) If you are not a local, and not an EU citizen, the only reason to choose Sweden over, say, the UK, US, Australia, or Canada for your studies would be that you have particularly strong, romantic feelings about Sweden, and, if you are planning to study at bachelor level, good enough Swedish to qualify for university entry (C1). If you are coming for your master’s degree, it would make sense if the study program in question is unique world wide. Other than that, there really isn’t much of a point. The fees for international students are comparable to those of English speaking countries. D) if you are a PhD student, no matter where from, you may find Sweden great to study in, for one because the research environment really is very good, and also because there will be no tuition fee charged - on the contrary, you get paid a salary that is good enough to live on. Now, before you jump up and start packing bags: This is PhD level we are talking about. You would be expected to have your master’s degree done before applying, in a capacity that makes you a logical candidate for the position as advertised. There will be fierce competition for each position advertised, and they will only accept the most suitable applicant. It’s very different from taking a PhD elsewhere - it’s a job. All that aside, studying in Sweden is nice. If I were to study all over again, I would do it here. The environment and facilities are very nice, the atmosphere and the level of professionalism very high, and the overall experience is on the whole a very positive one. I have also taught in England, France, Germany, China, India, and New Zealand; and I have studied in the US, Canada, and Germany. I think the closest to studying in Sweden come the German technical universities, the Fachhochschulen, as well as some private, French design schools. The focus is very much on employability and subject relevant skills development, availing itself of project based peer learning to a great extent. Structured, school-like, and in small groups with a good student/ teacher ratio that makes learning personal.

Question: Would you feel safer in Germany than Sweden?
Answer: Personally, I tend to feel nervous when I’m in Germany. The problem I have with it is the very outspoken nature of the people, and a lifetime of bad memories of bullying and being threatened by vigilante types who saw miscreants everywhere, myself included. If I had a dollar for every time someone shouted at me for some perceived misdeed, oh my. Neither place gives me the willies regarding crime though. I’ll happily go anywhere, any time. Just that, in Germany, I tend to be extra careful not to incense the wrath of someone who sees me as a villain, because they will lash out. I’ve been there. I’ve been threatened with physical violence for wearing tight fitting jogging attire in the inner city of Karlsruhe, I’ve been threatened to have my teeth bashed in by a colleague who didn’t like the way I was doing things, I was threatened with being beaten senseless by a tram conductor in Karlsruhe who thought I had my feet up on a seat (I didn’t), and I had a truck driver at a highway rest stop near Mannheim scream at me in the most colourful terms because he thought I had hindered his progress. Oh, and then, there was the guy who was going to punch my lights out in Pforzheim because I had the audacity of parking where I was parking - it was just a public parking lot. I have no idea what his problem was to this day, but I did report him to the police. Oh, and most recently, someone tried to rip my face mask off my face in Munich, shouting something about “total nonsense”. The sense of entitlement and a certain, culturally based willingness to get loud and physical makes Germany a pretty threatening place by my standards. I only go there to do some people a favour, these days. I find this picture a very good symbol for what it’s like: All very good to look at, but exclamation marks are overused.

The latter is probably what really kept me going. I realized quickly that it is very satisfying to make people laugh, so I turned from this silent little nerd to a stand up comedian, over night. I might have been seven or eight years old, and it was a chance discovery. My mum was putting my jeans into the washing machine, and had extracted a little toy pistol I had kept in it and put it on the machine. I happened to be passing by and asked politely whether I could have the gun, or if she still needed it. It was an innocent, politeness inspired thing to say, but hilariously off. That moment changed my life. I realized I could make people laugh by saying certain things. I made it my mission to do this as often as possible, and became a far more extrovert person.

Question: How many cats are too many inside?
Answer: I happen to have some first hand observations to offer on that question, and I think about 30 square meters per cat are required. Once upon a time, we lived in a semi detached house in Warrington, England, with our two local cats, Jessie and Aerial. The house had 92 square meters of living space, and the cats blended in just fine. Then I went to my parents’ place in southern Germany and retrieved my old Canadian cat Ozzie, who had been living with them for six years. Things became more snug, but still worked. We had three cats sleeping in our bed at night. Cozy, but no problem. And then, we somehow decided we wanted Aerial’s father, Billy, to move in as well. He was a Warrington street cat, and we always saw him on the fence in our garden. He was lovely, so we began to integrate him more into the household, and he took to it quite naturally. That’s him there, on the right. Now things began to feel a bit cramped. It also didn’t help that Billy and Ozzie didn’t get along so well, with Ozzie being a bit deaf, and Billy being a bit of a bully who didn’t like it when Ozzie didn’t react to his antics. So we had the odd altercation to contend with. Also, now there was a cat smell, noticeably in the air when I came into the house in the evening, despite diligent cat toilet management. So, keep it to one cat per 30 square meters, I would say.

Question: Can I, as an American, legally purchase a vacation house in Sweden?
Answer: Yes, you can. Home ownership is not dependent on citizenship in Sweden. The only challenge is to be able to keep that house alive without having a Swedish bank account, which requires a Swedish ID to apply for, and a Swedish “Mobile Bank ID” to operate online. Without these, and they would be pretty much impossible to obtain without having a social security number, which is in turn only available on the basis of employment, which in turn is dependent on a work visa and its not insignificant intricacies, you would need to resort to electronic monthly billing and international bank transfers for utilities and insurances. Which can be an issue with some smaller agents, such as the garbage collection people or the chimney sweep, who may not have international banking capability, and no IBAN or Swift numbers. I ran things in that way while living in England, maintaining my house in Sweden, and only managed because I had local friends I trusted I could regularly send money to in order to pay my stuff. The problem with that is that you must rely on someone else, and if they mess up, it can be difficult to fix. Also, any money sent to someone with a Swedish bank account will automatically find its way into their annual tax returns as an income, since the tax authorities use banking information to pre-formulate those, which means that those nice enough to help out will actually end up paying tax for it. So, buying is easy, but afterwards, it can be headache time.

Question: Do Swedish people look down on others who don't like to drink or socialize in bars?

Question: Is German food good?

Question: I’m currently in the US and I can’t take living here much longer. I’ve admired Scandinavia for a long time and very much want to move there. What’s the easiest way to do this?
Answer: If you have the citizenship of an EU country, you can actually simply turn up, get a job, and stay. Without that though, you would need a job offer of some heft to qualify for a work visa. It can be done. People do it all the time, but of course it is easiest for those who come with university degrees and experience in fields where there is a skills shortage, and it may well be that speaking the local language is a requirement, too. I’d say the non-EU workers who most easily get work visas tend to be IT specialists with bachelor- or master’s degrees and about five years of relevant work experience. There, it’s also not a big deal if your Swedish or Norwegian isn’t quite there yet. But there wouldn’t be much, if any, hope otherwise. Many would-be immigrants are making the mistake of thinking “if only I aim for a low enough level job, I might just make it in” - but that’s not how Scandinavia works. Any company sponsoring a foreign worker must make an offer that is on par with what they would offer a local in every way, but there is really no point in bringing in a part time cleaner from Nauru who speaks no Swedish or Norwegian when we have armies of unemployed people who have grown up here and know the ways, and the language. Question: What is something common with most product designers?
Answer: There tend to be two kinds of product designers: A) those deciding to study it; very often, almost as a rule, they would have been struggling with the natural sciences in high school, had above average, creative abilities, and frequently some learning issue like ADHD. I’m not saying these things make you a perfect product design student though. Clearly, it would be an advantage to have mastered the natural sciences, and not have a learning issue, but the thing is that we place much higher emphasis on creativity in this field, and less importance on the natural sciences, so people like that tend to naturally gravitate toward us. B) those who graduate and then become successful product designers; the more successful of my product design students all seem to have the following traits in common: Rational, professional, systematic, imaginative, calm, tireless. The natural home of product designers in industry is the R&D department of manufacturing companies, where one works with engineers, CAD operators, and technicians, very often building and testing prototypes. So these people need to be able to interface with all this, and remain attuned to the pace and the limitations of the enterprise.

Slipping into that is relatively easy - I found, for example, that a former contractor from my village had become an undersköterska at the local clinic. We are talking a guy who had, up until very recently, been putting roofs on houses, drove diggers around, and has a grade nine education from Poland. Other than that, hospital administration jobs may well be an option for someone who really is a doctor, as they would be deemed familiar with a lot of the things that go on there. Question: What do you think of the current ‘Sweden Gate’ trend on the internet? Sweden found itself at the centre of a massive debate as a post on social media about Swedes 'not feeding their guests' kicked off a massive online debate

Think I’m exaggerating? This is a sign on an entrance door of my university; it says that peanut products are no longer allowed, for safety reasons: Much fun has been poked at the Swedes for the overly serious way in which they react to what are often perceived to be small problems elsewhere. There is this old joke my Swedish teacher told me thirty years ago, illustrating the differences in mentality between the Nordics: “Let’s say some kid trips over his open shoelaces and hurts himself while walking in the street; a Danish passer-by would ask if the kid is ok, possibly offer some comforting words and a candy, and be on his way. A Finnish passer-by might assure himself the kid is ok, then teach him to tie his shoelaces properly. A Norwegian passer-by might check there is no serious injury, tell the kid a nice little story to take their minds off things, and send them on their way. A Swedish passer-by may very well call an ambulance and the kids’ parents, and then start a committee with research body and EU funding to address shoelace-induced street injuries, possibly feel inspired enough by the traumatic event to start a velcro company, and generally have some sleepless nights over this thing for years.” If there is any substance at all to the Swedengate story, this is the spirit in which I would take it.

Question: How do you keep your car windows from freezing overnight?
Answer: It’s actually surprisingly easy to keep your car windows from freezing. Frost is simply ice crystals accumulating on a surface, so put something on your windscreen in ways that it won’t blow away over night, and you’re all set. Some people jam a piece of cardboard under their wipers, but I have something better. It’s a piece of neoprene foam matting, not the cheapest kind maybe - about 0.8 cm thick, and I think the piece I have there is worth about 20 USD. I’ve put duct tape across it, with wine corks at the end. The wine corks dangle inside the car when I close the doors, and the neoprene foam shield covers everything, including the wipers. You need the wine corks so the duct tape doesn’t get pulled out. We get winds of about 50 km/h, and they can’t think of anything more fun than to rip some 20 dollar piece of neoprene off a Toyota and carry it all the way to Norway. Some people try it with these aluminium thingies originally intended to cover the dash boards of parked cars in Portugal or Brazil. Me, too. These things last about three days when the weather is clement where I live. Then, it’s tinsel. (the cable is for the block heater, by the way, and it also feeds the interior fan heater that’s on a timer to bring the car’s interior from minus 35 Celsius to a balmy ten or so before the trip starts). As for the cardboard solution, it’s great until you put your ice encrusted piece of cardboard inside the car to go home. Once you get there, it’s porridge. Where I live, frost is not just frost. This is some spiky stuff. Walk on it, and it sounds like breaking glass. Forget about cardboard or aluminium foil. Floor mats is what you’ll want. And duct tape, and wine corks. You’ll need four wine corks, by the way. Start the project by buying four nice bottles of good, Argentinian red.
